#7816. Your Home Flooded? Here’s Exactly What to Do Next To Minimize Damage

Parts of the U.S. are facing an increased risk of flooding. Here’s your no-panic playbook for if it ever happens to you.

As the warm air from a super el Niño makes its way across the North American continent, parts of the U.S. are facing increased risk of flooding in 2026 and 2027, according to Newsweek. The potential for disastrous wind and rain events during the winter is so great that the governor of California had already declared a statewide state of emergency as early as September. Southern states, from California to Florida, face the possibility of heavy rain, making flood response preparations even more important for people in these areas than in previous years.

Of course, you don’t have to wait for torrential rains to be at risk of flooding. A plumbing problem, like a toilet overflow, a burst pipe or a backed-up floor drain, can be just as serious. Whether your house flooded because of a natural disaster or a plumbing problem, timely response is of the essence to avoid mold and structural damage to your house and belongings as well as denials on your insurance claims.  The following checklist — informed by insurance and home restoration experts — will help you get ready.

“Water and electricity are the biggest immediate safety risk after a flood,” says damage remediation expert Sam Hickerson. Water flooding your basement or ground floor may come into contact with wall receptacles or other electrical equipment. If the power is still on, the water may be electrified.

Shut off the power yourself if you have a dry pathway to the main panel. If you have to wade through water to get to the panel, call the power company to have them do it remotely. Stay dry until you know the power is off.

Even after you’ve shut off the power, it’s important to stay out of the water, because it could be contaminated with sewage, animal waste and agricultural runoff. The bacteria, viruses and toxic chemicals these contaminants carry are obvious health hazards.

If the water is deep, there could be all sorts of debris in it that you can’t see, including broken glass and sharp metal. One false step, and you could suffer a cut that would be instantly infected if there are pathogens in the water.

“Many policies have specific windows for reporting flood damage, and delays can complicate a claim,” warns Hickerson. To avoid delays, call the insurance company as soon as it’s practical to do so and file a claim.

You don’t need to provide any details at this point; you’re just getting the claims process started. It will be the adjuster’s job to assess those details at some point in the (hopefully) near future.

Houston Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images

You’ll need photos to document the damage, and foundation repair specialist Shane McClintic recommends taking them before you start the cleanup. “Go around your house and film everything that suffered damage,” advises Gulf Coast flood insurance specialist Brad Spurgeon. “Once you have cleaned up your damage your pictures won’t be as useful to the insurance company.”

In particular, advises restoration expert Vinnie Guaderrama, take a picture of the highest point of water on the wall. “Always photograph the data plates with the model and serial numbers before you remove water heaters, furnaces, washers and dryers. Many people forget to do this, and it can be difficult to find these numbers at a later date.”

Try to have a restoration professional on site quickly. Restoration pros are in short supply during widespread disasters, however, so you might be working by yourself. If so, “work fast,” says McClintic.

According to the EPA, mold probably won’t grow on water-damaged materials if they dry within a 24-48 hour period. Once mold gets a foothold, it’s much harder to eradicate, so time is of the essence.

Because you need to work quickly to prevent mold from getting a foothold, water extraction should begin as soon as you can do it safely. “A wet/dry shop vac works for smaller amounts,” says Hickerson,  “but a sump pump is worth renting for anything beyond a few inches of standing water.”

When you can’t reach a hose into corners and under cabinets, don’t be afraid use a bucket and sponge to get the water out. Any standing water you leave will raise the room humidity and promote mold growth.

When you uncover previously submerged carpet, McClintic recommends either taking it outside or, if you can’t, pulling it back to air it out. “Prop up furniture on wood blocks to stop wicking,” advises Hickerson, “and pull baseboards, not just carpet, in flooded rooms.”

Drywall is a porous material that wicks water upward, and once waterlogged, you need to replace it. To avoid having to replace entire walls, McClintic advises cutting the drywall about a foot above the water line.

If you have valuable documents or photos,  Guaderrama suggests putting them in the freezer (if it’s working) until the house dries out. Strangely enough, the freezer is a low-humidity environment.

Run fans and dehumidifiers and, if it isn’t raining, open doors and windows to get air circulating and dry the space as fast as possible. Hickerson warns that things may look dry when they really aren’t, so he recommends keeping the fans running for at least 48 hours, and perhaps as long as 72 hours.

Once the area is dry, Florida restoration pro Darren Impson advises cleaning and sanitizing with an anti-microbial cleaner. He says you should call a restoration company for this, but it might be hard to schedule one immediately after a disaster.

If you do it yourself, the CDC recommends using dish detergent and water or one cup of bleach per gallon of water. Use bleach only on hard, non-porous surfaces. It doesn’t penetrate porous materials like wood and won’t reach mold embedded in them, so scrub porous surfaces with detergent until the mold is gone.

People often forget to look in HVAC vents, says Hickerson, and if they’re wet enough to support mold, the blower could contaminate the rest of the house as soon as the HVAC system turns on, despite your sanitation efforts.

Uncover any vents that were submerged, ventilate the ducts to dry them out, then sanitize the metal with a bleach solution (metal is non-porous, so bleach is effective). It’s best to wait until you’ve done this before you operate the HVAC system.

#7815. 5 Spots for a Water Leak You Might Totally Miss—But Can Cost You

Plumbing lines run throughout the home and the yard, bringing in fresh water for you to bathe, wash, water, and drink. However, when there is an issue with one of these plumbing lines or the attached appliances and fixtures, what seems like a small leak can quickly become a major problem as the growing accumulation of water causes water damage, encourages mold growth, and slowly ruins existing plumbing connections.

According to the EPA, the average household’s leaks can account for more than 9,300 gallons of wasted water per year, while some homes have leaks that waste 50 gallons or more per day. As a plumber and restoration expert, I have seen many issues that were easy enough to fix turn into major restoration projects simply because they were unseen or neglected for so long.

Even a single leak can destroy insulation, ruin drywall, and cause mold to spread behind your walls. Before your plumbing becomes a problem, use this guide to discover five water leak sources you might miss so that they don’t cost you in the long run.

Since this is a battery-powered unit, you don’t have to worry about missing a leak just because the power is out. Learn more in our buyer’s guide.

Water-carrying appliance hoses, like those on refrigerators, dishwashers, and washing machines, are notorious for causing catastrophic, hidden water damage. Since these appliances are often pushed tight against walls or tucked inside cabinetry, a slow leak can be difficult to find as it quietly rots the subfloor for months before a puddle ever creeps out into the open room.

The wax ring or plastic flange connecting the toilet base to the waste pipe can degrade over years. Instead of leaking onto the bathroom floor, the water can seep straight down through the subfloor, rotting the ceiling framing of the room directly underneath, which is why you need to be aware of any potential signs of a water leak, especially in the bathroom.

Water leaks caused by frozen pipes hidden behind walls or under concrete slabs can go unnoticed for a long time, causing extensive water damage in the walls if you aren’t careful. Water lines running beneath a concrete slab foundation can corrode or shift, causing a slow leak. These are highly hidden and usually only identified by a warm spot on the floor, a spike in the water bill, or eventual foundation cracking.

Underground irrigation lines are one of the most common culprits behind massive, hidden water loss. Because irrigation systems are buried across a wide outdoor area, an underground leak can dump thousands of gallons directly into the soil without ever creating a surface puddle.

Like roof leaks, outdoor spigots can lead to unexpected damage over a long period of time. These spigots should be turned off during the winter to prevent them from bursting internally during winter freezes. However, they may also develop leaks during the warmer months of the year, and the leak can remain completely hidden inside the wall cavity or crawlspace, only letting water escape whenever the valve is opened.

I was already a fan of the original Auk Mini after testing it for our guide to the best grow lights, so I was curious whether the new Auk Mini 2 actually improved on it or simply gave it a facelift. I tested the Espresso/Walnut model on the same kitchen counter where I used the original: an area that receives virtually no natural light. That meant the plants were entirely dependent on the Mini 2’s built-in grow light. I planted all four included pots with the supplied seeds, two basil and two parsley, and grew them for about a month.

The biggest change I noticed right away was the design. The original Auk Mini was already one of the best-looking growing systems I’d tested, but the Mini 2 feels more finished. Its corners are rounder, the transitions between components are smoother, and the whole thing has a more organic shape. I tested the Espresso/Walnut finish again, and it’s still my favorite. The pots have changed, too. Their bottoms are more rounded and extend farther into the reservoir, which appears to give the growing medium better access to water.

Setup is still wonderfully simple. Auk gives you exactly enough prehydrated coco coir for the four pots, and I’ve yet to use another coco coir product that’s as pleasant to work with straight out of the bag. I filled the pots, planted the supplied basil and parsley seeds, scattered the included (and new) small stones over the growing medium, added water and nutrients, and installed the light. That was basically it. The new top layer might seem like a minor addition, but germination and early growth seemed noticeably quicker than with my original Mini. Auk claims the Mini 2 produces 20 percent more growth, and while I didn’t conduct a controlled comparison, my experience certainly supports the idea that plants establish faster in this version.

After roughly a month, all four plants had grown into full, healthy herbs that I was able to harvest for cooking. That’s particularly impressive considering they received no sunlight whatsoever. I didn’t encounter algae, mold, or other growing problems during testing. Maintenance was minimal, too. During the first month as the plants were establishing, I didn’t need to refill the water reservoir.

Once the herbs became established and started drinking more, I simply topped off the reservoir as necessary. At that point, trimming the herbs to keep their growth under control actually became more work than maintaining the garden itself, and that’s hardly a complaint when the payoff is fresh basil and parsley whenever I want them.

There are other upgrades, including an optional app, a new Slow Mode, a larger reservoir, and optional pots designed for larger plants. Those additions make the Mini 2 more versatile, but I don’t think existing Auk Mini owners need to rush out and replace their current unit. The original is still really well made. My biggest complaint is that at $249, I wish Auk included the two larger pots and longer dowels rather than charging another $79 for them. Still, for someone buying their first Auk, I’d absolutely choose the Auk Mini 2. It’s super easy to use, grows plants effectively with minimal effort, and actually looks good while doing it.

We’ll help you set up your first garden—whether that’s a few pots on your patio, a raised bed, or an in-ground plot out back—and select the right plants for your soil and region.

#7812. Why You Should Pay Attention to Diamond-Shaped Signs on Trucks

Those metal diamonds on the back of trucks serve a purpose. Learn how hazmat placard holders work and what an empty one actually means.

Drivers have a lot to pay attention to on the road. They watch their speed, check their mirrors, and keep an eye out for sudden stops. But one detail most drivers probably haven’t given much thought to is the diamond-shaped designs on the back of trucks, even after seeing them countless times.

No, they aren’t decorations. It’s a small detail that serves an important safety purpose, especially if there’s an accident involving dangerous cargo. Learn how the holders work, what the warning signs mean, and why some appear empty.

They’re called hazmat placard holders. These metal frames hold warning signs that identify certain hazardous materials a truck might be carrying. The bare diamond in the photo is simply a holder. Its lines and clips don’t send any special message to other drivers.

Truck operators leave the holders attached and change the signs depending on their cargo. Some hold removable placards, while others have several signs that drivers can flip between. Labelmaster, a company that makes flip-placard systems, explains that drivers can change the warning without replacing the holder.

The placards use colors, words, and symbols to identify different hazards. Red often indicates flammable materials, while a black-and-white sign marked “CORROSIVE” warns about chemicals that can cause damage. Other signs identify dangerous gases, explosives, or toxic substances.

“Placards serve as an easily identifiable, visual source of information used by millions of workers in the transportation, public safety, and hazmat industries,” according to the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA).

These warnings help emergency responders recognize potential hazards during an accident or spill. Some placards also display numbers that identify specific hazardous materials.

An empty holder may mean the truck doesn’t need to display a warning for its current shipment. Trucking companies leave the frames attached because their vehicles might carry different types of cargo from one trip to the next. An empty holder doesn’t necessarily mean the truck isn’t carrying hazardous materials, though. Federal regulations don’t require placards for every hazardous material or quantity.

When trucks do need placards, PHMSA requires them on both sides and both ends of the vehicle. Carriers must also keep the signs secure, readable, and visible. Federal regulations also prohibit misleading signs that resemble official hazmat placards. The rules specifically mention “Any sign, advertisement, slogan (such as ‘Drive Safely’), or device” that could be confused with an official warning placard.

A bare metal diamond, however, isn’t a hazard warning by itself. It’s simply a holder for the appropriate sign when the truck needs one.

#7811. 10-Year "Harassment"/"Stalking" Sentence for Repeatedly Criticizing Police Detective Violated First Amendment, Amicus Brief Argues

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I was delighted to sign on to this brief in State v. McMenamy (Mo. Ct. App.) just filed by the ACLU of Missouri Foundation and the Wash. U (St. Louis) First Amendment Clinic, on behalf the ACLU of Missouri and Profs. Jane Bambauer and Lyrissa Lidsky and me. The Introduction:

The First Amendment and article I, § 8 of the Missouri Constitution broadly protect the right to speak to the public about other people. This is true even when the speech "is intended to trouble or annoy, or to make another timid or fearful." United States v. Sryniawski, 48 F.4th 583, 587 (8th Cir. 2022). And it is true even when speech uses "social pressure and the 'threat' of social ostracism … to embarrass others or coerce them into action." NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware Co., 458 U.S. 886, 910 (1982). While individuals who are the subjects of unwanted speech may be able to limit some speech directed to them, they cannot limit offensive speech about them directed to others. Organization for a Better Austin v. Keefe, 402 U.S. 415, 419 (1971).

Contrary to this established law, Matthew McMenamy was convicted and sentenced to 10 years in prison for openly and vigorously criticizing a local police detective he believed had engaged in misconduct. Mr. McMenamy used his public social media accounts and publicly distributed flyers to attempt to draw the community's attention to the detective's actions. He expressed his hope that his revelations would result in the officer's removal.

While Mr. McMenamy's speech was certainly concerning to the detective, the circuit court did not make any finding that either the flyers or any one of the dozens of social media posts submitted as evidence fell within any category of unprotected speech, such as true threats. Nor could the circuit court have done so, as none of Mr. McMenamy's speech was outside the bounds of the First Amendment's protection. His convictions for harassment and stalking violate the First Amendment and should be reversed.

The opening paragraph of the section on the facts (for the full discussion of the facts, read the brief):

In August 2023, Matthew McMenamy began posting on social media about what he viewed as misconduct and racism by a local police detective, who years before had been involved in Mr. McMenamy's involuntary commitment. See State's Exs. 60A–M. Mr. McMenamy sought to publicize one of the detective's public Facebook posts, where the detective wrote: "If black lives matter then why are they shooting and killing each other at an alarming rate." State's Ex. 60B ("Let's make this racist post go viral … #BLM #RacistCop ….); State's Ex. 60A ("The people want answers. Is [detective] a racist? Does he feel that people of color do not matter because of an idea that they murder each other at an alarming rate?"). Many of Mr. McMenamy's posts were aimed at sharing with the public his concerns about the detective's fitness for his position. For example, Mr. McMenamy posted he was "in talks with a billboard company to put [detective's] racist quotes up next to a picture of him in uniform" because "[s]omeone like that shouldn't be a detective, an election [sic] official, or let alone anything near public service." Tr. 736:10–21, State's Ex. 60K. Mr. McMenamy's posts also described his feelings about his prior involuntary commitment and thoughts about hurting his parents before getting help. See State's Ex. 60E (Mr. McMenamy's post that he "had a bad day last Sunday … I still need time to heal but … I am going to counseling and I will be looking for support groups").

And the opening material in the legal argument (again, read the brief for much more):

All of Mr. McMenamy's social media posts and his distribution of flyers were protected by the First Amendment. Harassment and stalking laws may, in some circumstances, be constitutionally applied to protect unwilling listeners from unwanted, one-to-one speech directed to that listener. The government's power to protect an unwilling listener from speech about them directed to the public, on the other hand, is sharply limited, even when that speech is annoying, offensive, or alarming. Unless such speech falls within one of the narrow, historically recognized categories of speech that the U.S. Supreme Court has held may be regulated without violating the First Amendment, such as "true threats," it is presumptively protected.

Here, Mr. McMenamy spoke to the public, and his speech did not fall within any unprotected category. This Court should reverse Mr. McMenamy's convictions. Even if this Court does not find that all Mr. McMenamy's speech is protected from criminal prosecution by the First Amendment, he is at least entitled to a new trial. The circuit court allowed the State to present evidence of more than four months' worth of social media posts to the jury and then instructed the jury it could find Mr. McMenamy guilty based on unidentified "alarming content" in these posts. This means a juror could have convicted Mr. McMenamy based on speech protected by the First Amendment.

[I.] The State's prosecution of Mr. McMenamy for harassment and stalking based on unwanted speech about individuals directed to the public violates the First Amendment.

Speech directed to the public at large is presumptively protected unless it falls into one of the narrow, historic exceptions to the First Amendment. This is because even if some listeners are likely to be offended, others may be willing listeners who find the speech valuable. For this reason, while harassment and stalking statutes may, in some instances, be constitutionally applied to repeated unwanted communications to an individual, they cannot be constitutionally applied to communications to the public about an individual.

[A.] Stalking and harassment statutes were originally intended to limit unwanted communications directed to a specific person.

For decades, laws have "restricted certain kinds of unwanted speech said to a particular person." For example, state and federal criminal harassment statutes were enacted to prohibit unwanted telephone calls to a particular person. Similarly, the federal government and some states have banned certain unwanted mailings into the home. These laws reflect an intention to protect individuals from repeated, unwanted communications to them, particularly in the home.

More recently, states enacted stalking laws to proscribe behaviors such as physically following, surveilling, or engaging in repeated unwanted personal contacts with a particular person. Courts have relied on stalking laws or restraining order laws to ban repeated or annoying letters, phone calls, or personal contact from a particular person. While some of these laws have been struck down in some states, "they have generally been upheld by lower courts; and the U.S. Supreme Court has upheld the federal ban on repeated unwanted mailings."

These laws share something in common: In the vast majority of their applications, they restrict unwanted speech to a person, not unwanted speech about a person. It is in this context—where the laws are being applied to "one-to-one speech"—that they "have generally been upheld against First Amendment challenge." Id.

As the internet has made it easier for communications to reach the public, maintaining this distinction between constitutionally permissible punishment of certain one-to-one speech and constitutionally impermissible punishment of one-to-many speech is critical. Social media is "the modern public square." However, the increased exposure for "upsetting" or "frightening" online speech can bring with it an increased risk of overcriminalization. Online communication "lack[s] many normal contextual clues," including tone of voice and expression. "The ubiquity of this speech raises the possibility of highly discretionary enforcement." Thus, in the context of online speech, courts must exercise particular caution to ensure the state's application of harassment and stalking laws does not exceed the laws' original intention or permissible constitutional boundaries.

[B.] The First Amendment grants broad protection to speech directed to the public at large, even when the subjects of that speech may be alarmed or offended.

The U.S. Supreme Court has consistently recognized a distinction between speech directed to the public at large and interpersonal speech for First Amendment purposes. Even when the content of the speech is subjectively offensive or alarming, the U.S. Supreme Court has typically protected public statements about a person—absent a showing of a narrow and well-established First Amendment exception, such as true threats, fighting words, or defamation.

As now-Justice Alito stated: "There is no categorical 'harassment exception' to the First Amendment's free speech clause." Saxe v. State Coll. Area Sch. Dist. (3d Cir. 2001); [citing other cases]. Many courts have endorsed this very point, quoting Saxe, in the context of criminal harassment laws and the closely related harassment restraining order laws. [Citing still more cases].

Unlike prohibitions on speech said to a particular unwilling listener, restrictions on speech to the public deprive a speaker of the opportunity to communicate with willing listeners. Denying access to potentially interested audiences undermines the use of speech to influence opinion and conduct and, as a result, hinders the robustness of public debate—particularly when the restricted speech concerns a matter of political, social, or other concern to the community. One's interest in being free from public criticism is insufficient to overcome protection for speech….

Accordingly, public statements about a person that coerce, annoy, alarm, offend, or embarrass are generally protected by the First Amendment. {The State may have some power to restrict narrowly defined categories of speech that reveals private information about a person that is "almost never relevant to any discussion on either public or private topics" (e.g., nude photos, Social Security numbers). No such speech is at issue here.} In Organization for a Better Austin v. Keefe (1971), a local civil rights organization believed a local real estate broker's practices were improper. After the broker refused to sign an agreement not to solicit property in the organization's community, the organization distributed leaflets critical of the broker's supposedly racist real estate practices at a local shopping center, on the doors of his neighbors, and to people going to and from his church. Some leaflets accused him of being a "panic peddler" that employed tactics to scare white homeowners into selling their properties; others encouraged recipients to call his home phone number to express their disapproval. The U.S. Supreme Court concluded that the organization's "inten[t] to exercise a coercive impact … does not remove [speech] from the reach of the First Amendment. Petitioners plainly intended to influence respondent's conduct by their activities; this is not fundamentally different from the function of a newspaper." The U.S. Supreme Court explained, "so long as the means are peaceful, the communication need not meet standards of acceptability," particularly where the target of the speech "is not attempting to stop the flow of information into his own household, but to the public."

While speech that is intended to solicit violence against particular people may be punishable, speech to the public that harshly criticizes its target or that attempts to persuade through social pressure does not lose its protection even if some listeners may react with threats or violence. In NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware Co. (1982), organizers of a boycott of stores owned by white merchants read aloud and published the names of Black residents who weren't following the boycott to place pressure on them. As in Keefe, the U.S. Supreme Court held the disclosures constitutionally protected, noting the First Amendment extended beyond abstract discussions to protect "offensive" and "coercive" speech intended to influence action. This was true even though some of the people who chose not to comply with the boycott were beaten, had their property damaged, or had shots fired into their homes. The U.S. Supreme Court explained that speech designed to persuade "through social pressure and the 'threat' of social ostracism … does not lose its protected character … simply because it may embarrass others or coerce them into action." …

For a couple of articles of mine on the subject, see One-to-One Speech, One-to-Many Speech, Criminal Harassment Laws, and "Cyberstalking" and Overbroad Injunctions Against Speech (Especially in Libel and Harassment Cases.

The brief was signed by Kristin M. Mulvey, Jonathan D. Schmid, Gillian R. Wilcox, Jason A. Orr (ACLU Missouri) and Lisa S. Hoppenjans, Benjamin J. Wilson, and students Lindsey Bennett. Megan McConnell (Wash. U. First Amendment Clinic).

Composting has numerous benefits, and having a compost tumbler makes the process even easier. This is a suitable size for medium to large gardens and landscapes.

The 65-gallon (8.69-cubic-foot) bin is made of UV-protected high-impact plastic. The frame is made of rust- and corrosion-resistant zinc-coated steel. It offers 15 inches of ground clearance for unloading compost via a cart.

We loved the size of this composter as well as its hand crank, which made it easy to turn even when the composter was full. We filled it with organic vegetable and fruit scraps, dry leaves, and dry grass.

This tumbler’s crank was a unique feature. Rather than having to roll the barrel, the crank allowed us to turn the bin with ease and “stop” it in a position where it was easiest to empty it. It is heavy, though, so users should be mindful of where to place it. Once it’s full, it’s difficult to move.

What our tester says: “I found this product to be high quality. It’s very durable, thanks in part to its rust-resistant zinc coating. Additionally, it’s relatively simple to assemble, and it’s easy to use.”—Jenn Ryan, Product Reviews tester and writer

Read our full review: RSI Maze Two-Stage Compost Tumbler

Get the RSI compost tumbler at Amazon, Lowe’s, Tractor Supply Co., or The Home Depot.

The FCMP Half-Size Rolling Composter is a compact, affordable pick ideal for one or two people who don’t generate much compostable waste. The ground-rolling design gives this unit a low profile that easily tucks away in small spaces, such as a balcony, patio, or garage. Built-in ergonomic handholds help make rolling less awkward. Aeration holes and deep fins break up clumps inside the chamber to maximize oxygen penetration.

The 19-gallon (2.5-cubic-foot) bin is made of recycled UV-inhibited BPA-free polyethylene. To speed decomposition, the manufacturer recommends turning the bin about twice a day.

The assembly of this product couldn’t have been easier. The composter came almost completely assembled—all we needed to do was place it on the stand and slide the door on. Although we loved the size and portability of this composter, it was too small for a large garden and would make a better option for urban composters, those with a small garden, or those who want to use compost for indoor or potted plants.

During testing, the composter needed to be turned frequently; for balance, using two hands was best. We also found it challenging to turn because it is not attached to the base; it merely sits on the stand, and both the stand and the composter can slide off balance. We found that the turning process was best done slowly, but people with mobility challenges may find this composter difficult to use, as it’s low to the ground and needs to be turned by hand.

We also found that the door was a bit tight and tricky to open and close when filling with compost and emptying. For emptying, the composter needs to be lifted, which can also be a challenge when it is full and heavy.

Overall, this composter makes a great option for those with smaller gardens, those who want zero-fuss assembly, or those who want a small but sturdy composter they can easily store out of sight.

Get the FCMP half-size compost tumbler at Amazon.

The Miracle-Gro Tumbling Composter provides a convenient place to recycle veggie scraps and houseplant debris while fitting easily into a small space. The hexagonal 18.5-gallon (2.47-cubic-foot) chamber features aeration holes and mixing bars for better oxygen infusion. Tight-locking slide doors keep out pests. For easy loading and unloading, toppers on the frame lock the bin rotation.

The UV-protected plastic chamber is built to withstand exposure to weather. The powder-coated stainless steel frame makes it easy not only to load, unload, and rotate the bin, but also to sweep or blow out debris from underneath. The composter requires some assembly, but that is made easy with step-by-step directions via a QR code. The package includes a pair of water-resistant, no-slip grip garden gloves.

Assembly for this composter was simple thanks to the included QR code that walked us through each step with 3D images—no app download required. We loved that this composter was easier to turn in a more compact size—perfect for one- or two-person households with small gardens or for urban gardeners. Since it is a smaller size, we found that the bin remained easy to turn even as it filled with compost. Its small size also makes it convenient for placing in a more conspicuous location as opposed to large dual-bin composters.

On the downside, we found that the door on this compost bin was a bit too tight and difficult to open with one hand. The frame of the composter is narrow, and combined with the fact that the composter is just inches from the ground means only a shallow dish or trough will fit under the frame to empty the compost. (In testing, we used an old sled for emptying and transporting the compost out of this tumbler.)

Get the Miracle-Gro compost tumbler at Amazon.

The RSI Maze 48‑gallon compost tumbler can be used for uninterrupted composting thanks to its dual-chamber design. The geared crank handle made turning easy, even when loaded. We liked its UV-protected barrel and galvanized steel frame, which are made especially for outdoor use.

Assembly posed a small challenge as some of the components were pretty tight and had to be forced into place. But once built, it worked smoothly and reliably. The sliding doors and ratchet lock held the drum in position, allowing easy collection of finished compost into a cart or bucket placed underneath.

The only drawback we noted was the assembly process, but that’s a one‑time obstacle worth dealing with as the daily ease and performance thereafter make up for it. Overall, the Maze tumbler delivers high usability with long-term value and minimal maintenance.

Get the Maze compost tumbler at The Home Depot.

We found the Genesis compost tumbler to be robust yet compact enough for backyard composting. We’re sold on its “rodent‑proof” design, too. Its secure sliding doors and solid construction succeeded in keeping the little critters out during our testing. We also liked the internal mixing rods and multiple ventilation points—the compost in this tumbler seemed to biodegrade more quickly than in the others we tested.

Despite its sturdy materials and tight assembly, we found it lightweight enough to rotate comfortably. Its design takes up only a small footprint but still offers substantial capacity. The UV-resistant barrel and powder-coated frame are built for long-term outdoor exposure.

On the downside, we think the doors could be wider, which would making loading and removing compost slightly less cumbersome. Still, for its build quality, ease of use, and continuous composting capability, we think the Genesis tumbler is a solid value.

Get the Genesis compost tumbler at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., or The Home Depot.

This tumbler earned its keep with a design built for efficiency and ease of use. Its dual‑compartment barrel allowed us to continue adding fresh scraps while older material matures in the opposite chamber. For anyone serious about continuous composting, a dual chamber is essential.

Made of steel, the two‑leg stand not only gives the tumbler a solid foundation but also elevates it off the ground, offering added protection against rodents. We found this model especially well made and sturdy.

We only had one gripe: the doors had a tendency to slide open at times as we rotated the barrels. Once, we were turning the handle while looking at something else, and we lost about half of our compost before we noticed. We ended up taping the doors shut to keep them closed. Still, it might just have been our model, and this tumbler is otherwise well-built.

Get the Exaco compost tumbler at Amazon, Lowe’s, The Home Depot, or Walmart.

With its built-in, wheeled tea-collecting base, the Good Ideas compost tumbler does double duty. It comes with a rugged, FDA-approved recycled plastic body, and upon arrival, it was fully assembled, so we didn’t have to put anything together. That was impressive.

Its twist-off lids provide a tight closure, backing up the manufacturer’s claims that it’s pet- and rodent-safe. We liked how durable and easy to use this model was from day one. It sits low, so there’s no chance of it blowing over in high winds. The compact yet spacious barrel is a boon for busy gardeners who want to produce a good amount of compost.

However, the large capacity means that once we got it full, rotating the tumbler required significant effort, as the material inside got heavier. Despite that, we think this model is likely to last for years, and with its compost tea collection, it’s a hard one to beat.

Get the Good Ideas compost tumbler at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., or Walmart.

We tested the best compost tumblers using a rubric that scored assembly, ease of use, and mobility when empty and full. We also noted the quality of instructions, including whether physical and digital versions were available. Each model was loaded with a mix of wet and dry compost materials—fruit and vegetable scraps, herbs, leaves, and grass—to evaluate how easy it was to turn under different conditions.

Points were awarded based on performance, with higher scores going to models that were simpler to assemble, turn, and empty. After testing, we averaged the points to determine our Best Overall pick and to rank the remaining models by their standout features.

Several characteristics can help shoppers determine which tumbler is the best composting tumbler for their needs. The type, intended use of the bin, amount of space available, and garden environment are some of the key considerations, as well as a few more, all detailed below.

Composting outdoors uses aerobic (i.e., oxygen-loving) microorganisms to break down organic waste quickly. Previously, home gardeners had to turn their compost piles manually with a garden fork to supply adequate oxygen. Compost tumblers, on the other hand, fully enclose the pile inside a vented barrel. They are mounted on a frame to make the barrel easier to turn, which eliminates the slow, back-breaking process of turning with a fork. The most important difference among the types of compost tumblers is in the way they turn. The tumblers rotate by one of three turning methods: ground rolling, central axis, and handle-operated.

A ground-rolling spinning compost bin has two separate pieces: the barrel (or bin) and the base. The base has a curved upper surface that cradles the bin, holding it in place without fasteners. Rollers built into the curved surface of the base allow the loaded bin to spin freely when pushed or pulled.

Because they sit at ground level, ground-rolling compost tumblers are a good choice for those who live in cold climates. The reduced exposure to wind and cold allows the bin to retain heat. The added warmth keeps composting microbes active instead of allowing them to go dormant in the cold.

Central-axis compost tumblers are built on a metal compost tumbler framework with an axle running through the midpoint of the bin. The framework serves two purposes. First, it elevates the bin to a height that reduces bending and stooping while filling, turning, and emptying the bin. Second, the axle allows the bin to spin freely to aerate its contents.

Central-axis compost bins are a good choice for those who suffer from back problems, since these bins allow the user to load and unload the material from a standing position rather than a stooping one. Some models also feature wheels, so users can easily relocate the bin to a different area of the yard or garden.

Handle-operated compost tumblers use gears to make turning the barrel much easier. The geared handle matches up with a gear built into the end of the bin. When the operator cranks the handle, it turns the bin in a smooth, controlled manner.

Handle-operated tumblers require less physical strength than other types of tumblers. This kind of tumbler might be a good choice for children, older adults, or gardeners with reduced physical strength. Buyers can also find a few electric composters that generate their own heat and are designed to be used indoors.

Before buying one, shoppers will want to determine exactly how they intend to use the bin. For instance, will it be used primarily for kitchen scrap disposal with a countertop composter like a Vego composter? Or, will it also process weeds, grass clippings, and other garden debris? Will it be filled irregularly, with additional content added periodically until it’s full? Or will it receive a steady stream of material on a regular basis?

For processing small amounts of kitchen scraps and occasional houseplant debris, a compost tumbler in the 15- to 25-gallon size range works well. To compost greater quantities on an irregular basis, such as at the end of a gardening season, large compost tumbler (50 to 80 gallons) can meet that challenge. For a steady stream of debris, dual composter tumblers can easily handle consistent loads, as they process and finish compost on one side while the user feeds new material on the other.

Indoor countertop models make good composting for beginners, since they do all the work for you. Using an indoor countertop model can let you see if composting is something you want to do on a larger scale.

Although some versions use steel, compost tumblers typically have an ultraviolet (UV)-protected plastic bin with a frame made of tubular steel or plastic. Since plastic resists both weather and corrosion and transfers heat slowly, it makes an ideal material for the bin.

Metal compost tumblers allow internal heat to escape more quickly in cold weather, slowing the composting process, and they can corrode over time. Tubular steel frames are the standard for central-axis and handle-operated tumblers. Most ground-rolling bins feature a plastic base, some of which include a reservoir for capturing the liquid runoff from the bin, called “compost tea,” another useful gardening medium.

Indoor models (like the Lomi Composter we tested) contain additional materials, such as silicone, that are designed to seal the unit, minimizing odor.

Bin capacity is measured in either gallons or cubic feet; 1 cubic foot equals 7.48 gallons. The smallest compost tumblers hold about 15 gallons, or about 2 cubic feet, while the largest holds more than 80 gallons, or 10.7 cubic feet.

Shoppers will also want to consider the amount of material and how often they want to compost. Typically, it takes at least 10 weeks to fully process a batch of compost. For this reason, many gardeners operate two tumblers simultaneously or use a dual-chamber tumbler. With a dual-chamber bin, users can add to one bin for 10 weeks, then close it, allow it to process, and gradually fill the second bin.

Tumbling helps provide air to compost and reduce moisture, both of which are vital in the decomposition process. Look for a compost bin with built-in aeration structures, such as air holes or vents in the walls, fins on the interior walls, flat sides, and mixing bars.

As the material inside breaks down, it can become compacted. Turning the bin loosens the material and breaks down the clumps. Air holes and vents allow the exchange of gases in the microorganisms within the decaying matter, letting excess moisture escape. Flat walls, such as in a hexagonal shape, force the material to tumble rather than slide. Additional texture comes from features such as fins and bars that help stir the material and add oxygen.

An enclosed compost tumbler also helps composters avoid pests like rodents and insects. The lids on these units thread, latch, or slide into tracks, which prevents rodents and other small animals from entering. Durable, heavy-duty plastic is difficult for rodents to chew through, and steel makes the bin virtually impossible to penetrate. Bears even find them challenging—though we don’t suggest putting that claim to the test if you don’t have to! Avoid adding animal favorites, such as meat scraps, bones, and items with high fat content, to the bin.

A foul odor emanating from the bin is an indication that the compost is either poorly aerated or that the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of the compost ingredients is out of balance. Compost tumblers are specially designed to deal with the first issue quickly and easily. Simply rotating the bin once or twice each week infuses oxygen into the mix and promotes the growth of beneficial aerobic-composting microbes. If the compost smells like rotten eggs, it needs air. In that case, simply spin the bin.

Just as keeping a pet requires consistent care and attention, so does composting, only in this case, the “pets” are millions of aerobic microbes. These microbes need a consistently warm, moist environment with the right kind of “food.” Their food initially consists of about 30 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen. Nitrogen comes from green compost ingredients, such as vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, and grass clippings. Carbon comes from so-called brown ingredients, such as autumn leaves, straw, sawdust, and paper. One way to ensure an adequate supply of carbon with kitchen scraps is to include paper products, like coffee filters, used paper towels, and tea bags, in the mix. When users add new scraps to the bin, they can cover the scraps with shredded newsprint or cardboard.

A properly working compost tumbler should heat up from the activity of the microbes and produce a somewhat sweet, earthy scent. If the ingredients are far out of balance, the microbes cannot process the compost efficiently, possibly causing unpleasant odors. If the mixture is slimy or has an ammonia odor, the nitrogen level is too high. It needs brown ingredients. If too much carbon is in the bin, it won’t heat properly; it needs green ingredients.

Compost tumblers offer numerous advantages over stationary compost piles. For starters, they’re neat. They enclose the mess for a tidier appearance. Moreover, they’re fast and easy to turn. Users only have to spin the tumbler for a minute or two instead of the half hour that it takes to turn a compost pile with a garden fork. Gardeners can move them into a garden shed or garage for efficient winter composting; however, a stationary pile simply goes dormant during cold weather.

Of course, different gardeners may have unique needs or physical limitations that impact how easily they can use a compost tumbler. Generally speaking, to distribute the compost, users can simply dump it from an elevated bin into a wheelbarrow. However, cold-weather gardeners who process compost outdoors may prefer a bin that sits directly on the ground. This is because a tumbler on an elevated frame would be exposed to cold on all sides; the composting process would slow down and stop with the rapid cool down. A bin directly on the ground would be insulated from that effect longer.

But some characteristics appeal to almost everyone. A wider opening makes it easier to load and unload, and, unlike latches and threaded lids, sliding covers rarely get clogged with debris. Exterior handgrips on the bin or a hand crank make it easier to rotate the bin.

There are several benefits of composting with a tumbler, with one of the largest draws being its impact on reducing landfill waste. On top of that, users get to take advantage of their own compost to promote a healthy garden, landscape, and houseplants. It also helps avoid the traditional downsides of composting: the amount of work involved, the mess and odors associated with it, the fear of attracting animal pests, and more. Compost tumblers eliminate these nuisances.

New to composting? Keep reading to learn more about using and maintaining your new compost tumbler.

Set up the outdoor compost tumbler in a sunny location to promote the rapid growth of composting microbes. Fill it (either all at once or over several weeks) with a mix of kitchen scraps, shredded newspaper, garden debris, grass clippings, fallen leaves, and other scraps. Moisten the mixture (it should feel like a not-quite-saturated sponge) and close the lid.

The time it takes to make compost varies depending on the temperature, time of year, and the balance of the ingredients inside. It’s possible to have garden-ready compost within 10 weeks if all of the right conditions come together.

For optimal processing and to eliminate odors, turn the compost tumbler two to three times per week—or more often if the manufacturer recommends it.

The compost should have the feel of a gently wrung-out sponge. As the material is processed and builds heat, moisture evaporates. Check the bin weekly and add water as needed.

Yes—at least we think so. Compost tumblers save time, reduce waste, and produce nutrient-rich compost faster than traditional piles. That being said, if you need compost and don’t want to wait, you can find bagged compost at garden and DIY centers.

Not usually—when properly sealed, compost tumblers deter pests far better than open compost piles.

Yes, air holes promote oxygen flow, prevent odors, and support the microbes responsible for decomposition.

Choose based on waste volume. We recommend opting for 15 to 25 gallons for small households, and 50+ gallons for large gardens.

Jenn Ryan is a freelance writer, covering many different topics, including green buildings, natural and sustainable skin care products, natural health remedies, and disease prevention—and she absolutely loves learning about new things through her work.

#7809. Why Do Construction Barricades Come in Different Colors? The Colors Decoded

Red, yellow, and orange barricades don't always mean the same thing. Learn what common safety colors signal and when to stay clear.

Yellow caution tape is a pretty familiar sight, whether it’s blocking off a wet floor or keeping people out of a construction area. Orange barriers along the highway and red warning signs at job sites are just as common. But barricade colors aren’t random, and they don’t all mean the same thing.

In the U.S., OSHA has rules for certain workplace safety colors, while ANSI provides guidelines for signs and warning tape. Road construction follows a different set of standards. Depending on the location, the same color might serve a different purpose.

Learn what the most common barricade colors mean, where people are likely to see them, and what to watch out for.

There’s a reason red is a common choice for warning signs. OSHA uses it to identify danger, emergency stops, and fire protection equipment. At a construction site, a red “Danger” sign might warn of exposed electrical equipment or another hazard that could cause serious injury. OSHA’s general-industry rules also call for red warning lights at barricades and temporary obstructions.

Of all the safety colors, yellow might be the one people see most often. It shows up on caution tape, warning signs, and around areas where crews are working. OSHA uses yellow to warn of physical hazards, including falls and falling objects. A damaged walkway or an area undergoing maintenance might have yellow tape around it.

There’s no shortage of orange around construction sites. On workplace warning signs, the color often identifies hazards that could cause serious injury, particularly around machinery or equipment undergoing repairs. Orange also makes road construction easier to spot. Crews use orange barriers and signs to warn drivers about upcoming work, lane changes, or other temporary traffic conditions.

Instead of warning people away from something, it usually helps them find safety equipment. A green sign might point toward a first aid station, identify emergency equipment, or provide instructions for workers. It’s especially useful in workplaces where people need to find these resources quickly.

Blue signs typically provide information about workplace equipment or procedures that don’t directly involve a hazard. For example, a blue notice might explain that a machine is temporarily out of service. Unlike red or yellow warnings, blue notices generally provide information rather than warn of immediate danger.

Purple isn’t a color people encounter very often on construction barricades, but it does have a specific safety use. OSHA requires certain radiation warning signs to feature the familiar radiation symbol in purple or magenta against a yellow background. These signs warn people about radiation hazards, including areas where access may be restricted.

Those orange-and-white striped barricades lining roads and highways aren’t quite the same as the warning signs used inside workplaces. The Federal Highway Administration has separate rules for these barriers, which crews use to close lanes, block roads, and direct traffic around construction.

There’s also a purpose behind the diagonal stripes. When a barricade directs drivers around an obstruction, the stripes slope down toward the side where traffic should pass.

OSHA, “29 CFR 1910.144, Safety Color Code for Marking Physical Hazards” OSHA, “29 CFR 1926.200, Accident Prevention Signs and Tags” ANSI, “Z535.1-2022: Standard for Safety Colors” ANSI, “Z535.5-2022: Safety Tags and Barricade Tapes” OSHA, “29 CFR 1910.1096, Ionizing Radiation” FHWA, “Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, 11th Edition with Revision 1”

#7808. Discovery Sanctions Recommended in "Are You a Jew? … Are You a Zionist?" Case

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The factual allegations, from a Sept. 2025 decision in the case by Judge Susan Illston (N.D. Cal.) (the case is Radice v. Jerusalem Boxing Club, LLC consolidated with the federal government's U.S. v. Harara):

The Jerusalem Coffee House [which Harara owns] is a business establishment open to the general public. The coffee house is located on the premises of the East Bay Community Space, "which regularly hosts events that are open to the general public for exhibition or entertainment …."

According to the complaint, on June 10, 2024, Michael Radice—who is Jewish—went to the East Bay Community Space "for the purpose of viewing the establishment for a fundraising event for his organization." Radice was wearing a dark blue baseball cap with a light blue Star of David and white Hebrew lettering. As he approached the community space from the side where the coffee house is located, a man sitting at a table in front of the coffee house asked, "Are you a Jew?" Radice answered in the affirmative. The man then asked, "Are you a Zionist?" Radice declined to respond.

The complaint alleges that "[t]he man then began shouting numerous accusations at Mr. Radice, including that he was complicit in Israel's military actions in the Gaza Strip following the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks and guilty of 'killing children.'" As Radice began to walk away, the man stood up and asked, "Where are you going?" The complaint alleges, "Mr. Radice saw another man, whom he later learned was Harara, walk out of the coffee house and speak to the man, and the two went inside." …

And now from Judge Thomas Hixson's Report and Recommendation yesterday:

There is no dispute that Defendant Abdulrahim Harara violated at least six discovery orders. Motion at 4-7 ("Harara has flouted at least six discovery orders," and enumerating the violations); Opp. at 7 ("But the question on this motion is not whether any order was violated; it is whether the record as a whole shows the kind of deliberate, deceptive obstruction that makes a fair trial impossible and justifies ending the case without one.")….

The real issue is what remedy the Court should impose for the serial violations of its discovery orders. The impact of Harara's conduct basically falls into three buckets: documents were produced late that should have been produced earlier; some document productions are incomplete; and there has been a wholesale failure to produce email. But having reviewed the voluminous evidence submitted in support of Radice's motion for sanctions, the Court thinks truth is available to the parties, and they should go ahead and have a trial on the existing record.

Harara's biggest failure in discovery is the nonproduction of email, and he does not have a good excuse. In many cases the total failure to produce email would justify terminating sanctions or at least adverse inference instructions.

But the Court is skeptical that this is such a case. The relevant events are alleged in-person refusals to serve Radice and another individual because they are Jewish. In other words, the relevant events did not occur by email. Before email existed, public accommodation discrimination claims like this were tried the old fashioned way: The participants in the alleged events testified, and the trier of fact decided who to believe. That option is still available here.

Email is still relevant, of course, because it could contain statements about what happened, or have evidence of the defendant's allegedly prejudicial intent. But here a lot of that type of evidence was produced in the form of Harara's text messages and social media feeds and other electronic records. These include a statement that seems to be by Harara that seems to say he throws pennies on the ground when Jews walk by; the coffee shop menu and outdoor signage with inverted red triangles, which Radice alleges is a symbol used by Hamas to mark Israeli targets in propaganda videos; the apparent introduction on the one year anniversary of the October 7 attack of a juice item named for a mastermind of the attack; a video of Harara telling a Jewish customer to leave because he had "a violent hat," referring to the Star of David on the hat; and a repost by Harara to his X account bearing the "Bay Area" screen name of a November 2, 2024 post calling that same Jewish customer "a genocidal, bottom dwelling Zionist scum" who "should be kicked out of every public establishment not just Palestinian owned ones!" There are also text messages that replicate the kind of thing a plaintiff would dream of finding in a defendant's emails—and certainly at trial Radice and the United States will argue these texts are strong evidence of liability.

Radice is certainly of the view that he has uncovered good evidence, even if it was produced later than it should have been, and even though it does not include email. See Motion at 15 ("The 6134 Bates-labeled pages and 2474 native files that Harara produced on or after August 7 include inflammatory documents that Harara willfully withheld until after discovery closed."); id. ("For example, a January 3, 2025 JCH Instagram post shows JCH advertising for sale a t-shirt featuring the Jerusalem Coffee House name ringed by flags with the emblem of Hamas, a designated terrorist organization dedicated to violence against Jews and Israelis."); id. ("His Instagram direct-messages contain both antisemitic tropes and antisemitic slurs.").

With all this evidence, can it really be said that Harara's failings in discovery have prejudiced Plaintiffs to such an extent that a meaningful and fair trial is no longer possible? That adverse inferences are needed because there is not enough evidence for the trier of fact to reliably draw conclusions about what happened?

No. These cases are about whether a coffee shop committed discrimination, and Harara has produced enough documents that Radice and the United States have what they need to go to trial. Even with the nonproduction of email, it is not true that discovery failed or that truth cannot be ascertained. The public policy in favor of deciding cases on the merits applies here.

Accordingly, the Court RECOMMENDS that the district judge DENY the request for terminating sanctions because there's just no need or basis for it. The Court DENIES the request for adverse inferences because it is essentially a request for a directed verdict. Each side should put on their case at trial, and truth should be determined in the normal way. There is no reason for the Court to stack the deck.

But that doesn't mean Harara escapes sanctions. He needs to pay for what he did. His serial violations of Court orders significantly drove up Radice's cost of litigating [the case]. Radice requests $166,500.50 against all Defendants. The entity Defendants have been in default during the period of time when Harara violated the Court orders, so are not the cause of Radice's increased legal expenses, and therefore will not be sanctioned.

Plaintiff's counsel's rates are reasonable. However, both the Benesch and ADL attorneys seek fees for work that preceded the violations of the Court orders, a problem that requires deducting about a third of the Benesch time and about a fifth of the ADL's time. That brings the total down to $118,000. In addition, even though Harara violated multiple discovery orders, it is also true that Plaintiff's counsel litigated [the case] with excessive ferocity. At times it seemed they were not just litigating a discrimination case but were out to destroy Harara. As a result their fees were excessive. The Court estimates that about half of the fees Radice incurred during the time when Harara was violating the discovery orders was due to the violations and the other half was for work that would have needed to be done anyway or that should not have been done at all because it was excessive. Accordingly, the Court SANCTIONS Harara in the amount of $59,000 and ORDERS him to pay that amount to Radice within 30 days.

In his opposition, Harara proposes some remedial measures. However, the Court will not adopt any of them. The proposal to remedy the lack of email production presupposes that Harara will have a lawyer to represent him. Opp. at 16 ("The full inbox Mr. Harara exported on September 3, 2026 will be reviewed by counsel, consistent with the Court's ruling that counsel rather than Mr. Harara conduct that review. That counsel will be either counsel Mr. Harara retains or volunteer limited-scope counsel appointed through the Court's Federal Pro Bono Project under General Order 25, to which Mr. Harara respectfully requests referral. Since his counsel withdrew, Mr. Harara has contacted lawyers and legal organizations and has not found a lawyer who will take his case."). However, Harara's inability to work cooperatively with two sets of counsel means this is an unrealistic proposal. And if no lawyer represents him, Harara's proposal contains no particular deadline by which emails would be produced. Opp. at 16 ("If counsel has not been retained or appointed within 30 days of the Court's order, Mr. Harara will file a status report every 14 days thereafter. In all events, the production under this paragraph will be complete within 90 days of the Court's order; if it is not, Mr. Harara will show cause why not, and the Court may then impose such further measures as it finds appropriate after notice and an opportunity to be heard.").

Harara's proposal to serve further interrogatory responses is highly unlikely to achieve anything. And there is no need for a further deposition of him; Plaintiffs' counsel can cross-examine him at trial….

Before choosing the best heater for the garage, take a few minutes to learn about some of the most important shopping considerations, including heating method, fuel source, and heat output. There are also critical safety features that can help keep users safe while enjoying a garage heater.

DIYers will want to determine what’s most valuable in their garage: freed-up space on the counter or the floor, or the ability to work at a few different workstations. Knowing this should help when deciding whether to purchase a stationary or a portable garage heater.

Busy DIYers may appreciate being free of the trip hazard that electric cords on the floor can create. Stationary garage heaters most often attach to the ceiling, but there also are options that mount to a wall.

There are a wide variety of energy options, sizes, and prices that range from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars. The downside to mounted heaters is that they typically cost more than their portable counterparts because they’re closer to commercial quality.

No matter the type of heating or fuel used, portable heaters focus warmth where it’s needed the most. Like space heaters on steroids, forced-air options feature large horizontal tubes that house the heating element and a powerful fan that delivers blasts of hot air.

While portable electric units often cost less, they can be less powerful than their multifuel counterparts. Alternatively, portable units can distribute warmth through radiant heat and convection.

Not all garage heaters control the temperature in the same way. There are three primary heating options: forced air, convection, and radiant.

Consumers have a wide range of energy options from which to choose when shopping for a garage heater. While heaters are most commonly fueled by electricity, propane, or natural gas, there are also those that run on diesel and kerosene.

Since electric garage heaters pull a lot of power, these usually require a designated electrical circuit on its own breaker. An electrician can tell if existing garage wiring is adequate to run an electric heater or if a new circuit should be installed.

If there is already natural gas service to a home, there is an option to install a natural gas heater. Propane-powered heaters can be installed on a home’s propane line, or individual tanks of propane to fuel smaller heaters can be purchased.

The best garage heater for a space can produce enough heat to be comfortable, without breaking the budget. Heat output for gas-powered heaters is measured in BTUs. Gas garage heaters typically range from 12,000 to 30,000 BTUs or more.

When trying to determine the heat output of an electric heater, a general guideline is to provide 10 watts of output for approximately every square foot of space. For example, a 100-square-foot room will require a heater with 1,000-watt output for adequate comfortable warmth.

Most heaters advertise the maximum square footage the unit can adequately heat with a standard 8-foot ceiling. If a garage has a higher ceiling, take that into consideration and pick a size up. Insulation will also affect the warmth factor in a garage. Even a high-capacity heater cannot prevent icy drafts from entering through poorly insulated doors and windows.

Safety must be a primary consideration when deciding on the best garage heater. To help keep the space safe and comfortable, manufacturers have added several features, including cool-touch exteriors, overheating protection, and automatic shut-off systems.

Various different features may add to the convenience and efficiency of a garage heater. These include programmable thermostats, oscillation, and remote controls.

Portable garage heaters only need to be positioned and provided with fuel or electricity to function. Wall- and ceiling-mounted garage heaters typically come with the hardware required to install the heater, but some products don’t have mounting brackets. Also, for hard-wired installations (these heaters don’t have plugs), it may be necessary to hire an electrician.

Mount a heater in the coldest corner of the garage, ensuring that ceiling-mounted models are at least 24 inches from the walls to reduce fire risk. Direct the heater toward the center of the garage and follow the manufacturer’s steps to make sure that the heater is installed according to its specifications.

Even after becoming familiar with the best garage heaters, there may still be some lingering questions about the type, efficiency, and appropriate size. Below are answers to some of the most commonly asked questions about garage heaters to provide additional info.

The best type of heater for the garage depends on your needs. Large garages benefit from a natural gas or propane heater because of the high heating capacity, allowing the heater to adequately warm the space. However, an electric garage heater is a safer alternative and the heating capacity is suitable for smaller garages.

Depending on where you live, the answer to this question can vary. Areas with mild winters will naturally require less heat production to warm a space than locations with harsh, freezing winters.However, an electric garage heater with 3,000 watts is usually needed to heat a 2-car garage. The best gas garage heater for a 2-car garage typically has a rating of about 18,000 BTUs to adequately heat the space.

Efficiency can be difficult to determine because an electric infrared heater technically has 100 percent efficiency, but it may actually cost more to operate than the best natural gas garage heater. This is due to the cost of electricity over natural gas or even propane. If you are looking for a heater that uses almost every watt of energy for heating, then an infrared heater can be the best option.

Yes, a garage heater can be too big. If it is too big, the excess heat produced quickly makes the garage feel uncomfortable, forcing you to open the door to release some heat. If you have a smaller garage, consider using a portable heater to keep the space warm.

It depends on the size of the garage. Typically, a good general guideline for electric heaters is that they provide 10 watts of output for every square foot of space. This means that as long as the garage is 150 square feet or smaller, a 1,500-watt heater is more than adequate.

Portable garage heaters can be placed anywhere. Fixed or mounted garage heaters should be installed in the coldest corner of the garage, directing the heat and airflow toward the center of the space. Make sure that heaters are installed at least 24 inches away from the walls, and always check the manufacturer’s directions so you install and use the unit properly.

#7806. Bonfire Season Is Here — Here Are the Dos and Don’ts for Staying Safe

How to not to expose yourself to toxic fumes, burn down the neighborhood and injure the kiddos, plus other tips for enjoying a stress-free bonfire.

Cool fall evenings naturally put our minds on the merits of bones-warming bonfires. And while many create cherished family memories and set the backdrop for festive community events, some end up in tragedy, with emergency room visits and property damage.

“Every season there are always the same preventable mistakes made that lead to injuries,” says attorney Kevin Henrichson. “Falling into the fire, using gasoline, adding fuel when you shouldn’t, failing to supervise children and consuming alcohol all raise the stakes of something bad happening.”

Ahead, experts walk through exactly what to do and not to do to stay safe while enjoying a bonfire.

Notify your local fire department of your plans and ask them for guidance concerning:

“One phone call to the fire marshal’s office takes two minutes,” says fire and home safety expert Eugene Klimaszewski. “Otherwise, the consequence of burning without a permit on a restricted day is a fine, and if it gets away from you, it’s your liability.”

Look for a flat, open spot away from fences, barns, houses, trees and ground vegetation. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) recommends keeping bonfires at least 25 feet from the house and other structures.

“That number isn’t arbitrary,” says Klimaszewski. “Radiant heat and drifting embers are what ignite a deck railing, a vinyl fence or the mulch bed against the house. Every ember that lands on a roof or in a gutter full of dry leaves is a coin flip. Most go out. The one that doesn’t becomes a structure fire.”

Build the fire downwind of your home and close all windows and doors on the fire side, to prevent smoke from getting in.

“Even a small amount of smoke reaching an indoor smoke detector is enough to set it off,” says Klimaszewski. If you have a monitoring system, that could trigger a call to the fire department. “At best that’s an embarrassing conversation with the engine company. In towns that charge for repeat false alarms, that’s a bill on top of the embarrassment,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you have an older home, which isn’t airtight, put your alarm system on test mode or notify your monitoring company about your bonfire plans.

Wind can carry embers up to a mile, which means a bonfire on a windy day can easily end with a wildfire or house fire. If your planned bonfire day turns out to be windy, reschedule it. And even if there isn’t a breeze, plan for one by clearing all debris from around the fire pit and building rocks or bricks up higher on the windy side, which protects the fire from the wind plus radiates heat toward you for extra warmth.

Kiln-dried wood is the best. Seasoned hardwoods like oak, cedar and hickory are particularly good because they burn cleaner, longer and hotter than soft woods like pine and aspen (though a little soft wood kindling makes starting a fire a lot easier).

Steer clear of gasoline or other accelerants, as they too often lead to burn injuries, out-of-control fires and noxious fumes. (One year, my neighbor used so much gasoline to start a bonfire that the resulting shock wave from the explosion knocked pictures off of people’s walls three blocks away).

“A lot of people think they can use gas or lighter fluid to get the fire started or revive it, but please never do that because the vapors can flash back and get everyone nearby,” says Henrichson. “Gasoline is particularly dangerous and should never be used to start or revive a fire.”

Pro-tip: If you struggling to start a fire, build up a good kindling base and use a campfire starter or small bit of tightly twisted newspaper. Ample kindling will help you get a hot coal-bed established, which will burn larger logs more effectively plus lessen smoke.

Avoid newspaper, cardboard and other paper products, which tend to break down into large flying embers. Also, never burn anything with adhesives, plastics and other chemicals. The health risks of this are obvious, but plastics and chemicals are hiding in many items you might not realize, including: dryer lint, food packaging with shiny ink, glossy magazines, pressed woods including butcher block, varnished furniture and clothing made with synthetic fibers.

Before lighting the fire, set up a water source in case embers become a problem. That will also make it easier to put it out completely when you’re done. NFPA actually requires a hose, bucket or extinguisher be on hand for all recreational fires, and for fires to be attended at all times.

“A fire that’s left alone for ten minutes while everyone goes inside for more drinks is the one that ends up on the local news,” says Klimaszewski. “And an unattended fire that spreads is the homeowner’s liability, full stop.”

Assign someone to supervise the flames at all times to prevent the fire from getting out of control, and to keep kids and pets from standing too close. Equip the supervisor with proper protective clothing, including a fire-resistant glove, long-handled poker tool, shovel, closed-toe shoes and eye protection.

“The most common injuries I’ve seen are from people falling into the fire, and young children are vulnerable to this because they may want to play in the area where everyone is hanging out by the fire,” says Henrichson. “There should be a no-enter zone that is explained to children every single time, and the person tending the fire should not have any alcohol.”

Watch for loose sleeves, blankets, boots and other combustibles that are too close to the fire. “Those fun marshmallow-roasting memories are great to make, but shaking a burning marshmallow can cause trouble, and if you use metal skewers, they can burn you too,” says Henrichson.

Also, know what to do beforehand if something ends up catching fire. “The old advice that we were told years ago is still true: stop, drop, and roll if your clothes catch fire,” says Henrichson. “Repeat this as necessary every time kids approach, because they don’t always know to stay back.”

Embers can easily reignite hours or even days later, so the best practice for putting out a bonfire is to drown it, stir the ashes, and then drown it again until everything is cold to the touch. Don’t cover embers with dirt, as that actually insulates them, leaving open the possibility for them to reignite if they’re uncovered by a stiff wind.

Pro-tip: Put ashes in a metal container with a lid, on a non-combustible surface, away from the house, garage and deck for several days before they go in the trash, says Klimaszewski. Never put them in a plastic bin or next to the house.
