#7716. The Logic of Voting for a Lesser Evil - and Other Writings on the Ethics of Voting

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Compendium of links to some of my writings on the morality of voting.

Tomorrow is election day. And - to put it mildly many of the options before voters are far from wonderful.  In all too many races, the candidates with a realistic chance of winning are all bad. This situation, like other recent elections, raises difficult questions about such issues as whether people have a duty to vote, whether it is permissible to vote for a badly flawed candidate if the alternative is even worse, and how to balance competing issues in making voting decisions.

I've written about these kinds of issues in some detail, previously, and this post links and and summarizes some of those writings. This is not a post about which candidate you should vote for in any given race. I've already written a post about why - in most cases - the Democrats are the lesser evil in races for federal offices this year (state and local elections are often a different matter). I've also written about why libertarians (like me) should seek political alliances with "abundance liberals" and why the previous "fusionist" alliance with conservatives probably cannot and should not be revived in the near future.

This post doesn't argue for any particular voting choice, but rather compiles pieces about  how we should make such decisions in general - and whether we should make them at all. Much of the post is adapted from a similar one I put up in 2024. Unless otherwise noted, these pieces were all published right here at the VC blog:

1. "The Logic of Voting for a Lesser Evil"

This post was inspired by the 2016 election, but almost all of it remains relevant today. In it, I explain why it is both permissible and desirable to vote for the lesser evil in an election where all of the viable options are bad. I address a variety of counterarguments, including claims that voting for a lesser evil makes you morally complicit in that candidate's wrongdoing, arguments that it's better to cast a "protest vote" for a candidate that has no chance of winning, arguments based on the very low probability that your vote will be decisive, and more. Here's a brief excerpt:

Imagine an election where the only options are Queen Cersei from Game of Thrones, and Sauron, the Dark Lord from Tolkien's Lord of the Rings. If Cersei wins, she will kill many innocent people, and oppress others. But she will leave much of the population more or less alone (as long as they don't openly oppose her or threaten her family in any way). If Sauron wins, he will kill far more innocent people, and make the survivors his slaves.

You can instead cast a protest vote for a vastly better alternative, such as Gandalf….. But, by assumption, these are purely symbolic options, because they have zero chance of prevailing. If the protest voter would otherwise have backed Cersei, the net effect of his decision to protest is to increase the likelihood of the worst possible outcome: the triumph of Sauron.

Under those circumstances, it seems clear that a person who ensures a Cersei victory has done a good deed. He or she will have saved large numbers of people from slavery or death, even though the Cersei regime would be a deeply unjust one.

The Cersei-Sauron hypothetical was obviously inspired by the contest between Trump and Hillary Clinton, and is an exaggerated version of that tradeoff. But I think it works for many other elections, as well - including many of the choices  voters face this year.

Notice how my logic is different from that of those who say you can only vote for a candidate if he or she meets some minimal threshold of character or good policy. On my approach, it is morally justifiable to vote for almost any candidate - even a cruel despot like Cersei - so long as the only feasible alternatives are even worse.

Canadian columnist John Robson responded to my piece in the National Post, and I, in turn, posted a rejoinder.

2. "Justifying a Moral Duty to Vote is a Lot Harder than You Might Think."

Many people, including some political theorists, believe we have a moral duty to vote. I disagree. Indeed, I think - in many cases - it's better if you don't vote, especially if ignorance and bias make it likely you will make a bad decision. Casting a ballot motivated by ignorance and bias is often worse than not voting at all.

3."Is there a Moral Duty to Vote in an Election Where the Stakes are Unusually High?"

Even if there is no general duty to vote, perhaps we are morally required to do so in situations where the stakes of an election are unusually high. In this post, I explain why I disagree - at least with respect to most voters. There is, however, a limited kernel of truth in this argument. An excerpt:

There is a kernel of truth to the claim that you have a duty to vote if the stakes are high enough. But the resulting moral duty applies far less often than advocates of the argument tend to assume. And the same reasoning actually implies many people have a moral duty not to vote.

Let's start with the kernel of truth. Imagine there's an election for a powerful political office that pits Gandalf (the benevolent wizard in J.R.R. Tolkien's Lord of the Rings) against Sauron, the despotic dark lord from the same story. If Sauron prevails, millions of people will die or be enslaved, while Gandalf would rule justly if he manages to win. And all you have to do to ensure Gandalf's victory is check his name on a ballot. If you do so, Gandalf wins; if not, Sauron does.

In this scenario, it seems like you have a moral duty to vote for Gandalf, at least barring some kind of extraordinary exigent circumstance. In a real election, of course, the odds that your vote will make a difference are far smaller than in this stylized example….

However, a large enough difference between the two candidates could potentially justify a duty to vote for the "right" candidate, even if the odds of casting a decisive ballot are very low….

But notice that the duty in question is not an obligation to participate in the process for its own sake. It's a duty to help good triumph over evil in a situation where you can do so at little or no cost. If you have a moral duty to vote for Gandalf in these types of scenarios, it follows that you also have a moral duty not to vote for Sauron. Indeed, the person who votes for Sauron is more worthy of condemnation than the one who merely abstains. The former is actively helping evil win, while the latter "merely" chooses not to help stop it.

While Gandalf supporters may have a duty to vote, Sauron supporters actually have a duty to abstain from doing so. Ideally, they should stop supporting Sauron entirely. But they at least should not take any actions that increase the likelihood of his victory.

All of the above analysis assumes that the voter knows which candidate is superior and to what degree. But, in reality, we have widespread political ignorance, and most voters often don't even know very basic facts about how government and politics work. Most are also highly biased in their evaluation of the information they do know….

Unless and until a voter becomes well-informed about the issues and at least reasonably objective in his or her evaluation of political information, she has good reason to question her judgment about which candidate is superior, much less by how much. Thus, she cannot conclude she has a duty to vote to help the "right" side win. She may instead have a presumptive duty to abstain from voting until she meets at least some minimal threshold of political knowledge….

Later in this piece, I note some possible exceptions to situations to the presumptive duty to abstain; there are unusual situations where ignorant voting really is better than no voting, and even unusual situations where ignorance leads to better decisions than knowledge (I expand on the latter possibility in greater detail in Chapter 2 of my book Democracy and Political Ignorance). I also address some other caveats and counterarguments.

Some steps you can take to be a better voter, building on a helpful article in Scientific American. I think a wide range of people can do these things. You don't have to be an academic or policy expert to undertake the task. But I am skeptical that more than a small fraction of the electorate will ever be willing to put in the time and effort.

In this post, I make a tentative argument for letting children vote, so long as they show they have attained a level of political knowledge as high as that of the average adult voter -which is not that high a standard! I expanded on the idea here. I do note the crucial caveat that it may not be feasible to do this, because it's possible government can't be trusted to come up with an objective knowledge test for the children (though we do in fact impose such a test on immigrants seeking to become US citizens). Letting knowledgeable children vote is one of my least popular ideas (which is saying no little, given how many other unpopular views I hold!). But I remain unrepentant about it. My 11-year-old daughter is one of the relatively few fans of this policy.

My proposal should be differentiated from the idea of letting parents cast votes on behalf of their children, endorsed by Republican VP candidate J.D. Vance, among others.

6. "Top-Down and Bottom-Up Solutions to the Problem of Political Ignorance," in Hana Samaržija and Quassim Cassam, eds. The Epistemology of Democracy (Routledge, 2023).

Many of the most serious flaws of voting arise from the fact that most voters tend to be ignorant about government public policy, and highly biased in their evaluation of the political information they do know. In this article, I go over a range of possible strategies for mitigating this problem. Here's the abstract:

There is broad, though not universal, agreement that widespread voter ignorance and irrational evaluation of evidence are serious threats to democracy. But there is deep disagreement over strategies for mitigating the danger. "Top-down" approaches, such as epistocracy and lodging more authority in the hands of experts, seek to mitigate ignorance by concentrating more political power in the hands of the more knowledgeable segments of the population. By contrast, "bottom-up" approaches seek to either raise the political competence of the general public or empower ordinary people in ways that give them better incentives to make good decisions than conventional ballot-box voting does. Examples of bottom-up strategies include increasing voter knowledge through education, various "sortition" proposals, and also shifting more decisions to institutions where citizens can "vote with their feet."

This chapter surveys and critiques a range of both top-down and bottom-up strategies. I conclude that top-down strategies have systematic flaws that severely limit their potential. While they should not be categorically rejected, we should be wary of adopting them on a large scale. Bottom-up strategies have significant limitations of their own. But expanding foot voting opportunities holds more promise than any other currently available option. The idea of paying voters to increase their knowledge also deserves serious consideration.

I expand upon the foot-voting approach to mitigating political ignorance in more detail in my book Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom. I also recently summarized and extended my ideas on this score in "Strengthen Democracy by Empowering People to Vote with their Feet," an article for the NYU Democracy Project, reprinted as a book chapter in Democracy's Challenges: I00 Ideas, (Robert Bauer, Samuel Issacharoff, Richard Pildes, and Rosa Po, eds., NYU Press, 2026).

How to decide which issues to prioritize over others. Not solely about voting. But highly relevant to voting decisions.

8. "If You Don't Vote, You Still Have Every Right to Complain."

Feeling down after considering the above? This piece might make you slightly happier; even if you don't vote, you are justified in criticizing the policies of the winners! I would add that the same logic shows that, if you vote for the winner on the grounds that she is a lesser evil, you are still justified in complaining about her policies. Vote for Cersei over Sauron, when necessary. But then condemn the evil she does. Just make sure not to be at the wrong place at the wrong time when she decides to purge her critics.

NEXT: Full Court Denies DOJ Petition In California Election Case In About 7 Hours, No Reply Needed

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7715. First-year attorneys average $131K at plaintiffs firms, new study finds

First-year attorneys receive an average of $131,313 per year at plaintiffs law firms and might receive a wide range of raises and bonuses, according to the National Plaintiffs’ Law Association’s inaugural salary report. (Photo by Andriy Onufriyenko/Getty Images)

First-year attorneys receive an average of $131,313 per year at plaintiffs law firms and might receive a wide range of raises and bonuses, according to the National Plaintiffs’ Law Association’s inaugural salary report.

The study, which surveyed 80 plaintiff-side attorneys in late 2024 and early 2025, found that the salary amount corresponded to the size of the firm. Plaintiffs firms with more than 100 attorneys averaged $160,857 per year, while those with fewer than 20 averaged $106,111 per year.

In addition, the study found that bonuses averaged $21,195, with the median for bonuses at $15,000.

While 21.5% of firms surveyed had no policy on structured or lockstep pay raises, about 49% did. Nearly 17% had a purely discretionary or merit-based raise structure.

#7714. Nika Grace on finding remains in deserts and writing a serial killer novel

It is a truth universally acknowledged that if you hike across the desert, intently looking at the ground, you will eventually find a dead body.

Let me back up a step to explain why an otherwise mentally healthy thirty-something woman would be hiking across the remote desert for so many thousands of trailless miles. It was because of #VanLife, actually, though this occurred before I understood how to use a hashtag (do I yet understand how to use a hashtag? Don’t answer that.) And, of course, I was never quite affluent enough to purchase a van.

The year was 2010. My husband and I had gotten married, acquired a mortgage, a master’s degree, and a matched set of Real Actual Careers. Reader, I lasted six months.

After that, I decided that business casual blouses and working for the weekends wasn’t for me, and we went on the run. We moved into a Toyota Tacoma truck nearly as old as we were, and worked seasonally to pay for enough ramen to keep rock climbing until we were too old and too square to get up the cliffs anymore.

After a short stint on the ice in Antarctica—a tale for another time—we landed in the Mojave Desert, tracking desert tortoises across the desiccated landscape. When I first got the job, I thought the stories of other tortoise bios finding dead bodies were some kind of urban myth. A form of hazing the new girl that was probably blown out of proportion thanks to mis-identified coyote bones and having too much time to think. Until we found a finger.

A woman’s finger; painted fingernail. No blood. No body.

It was found by a cheerful ex-raft-guide from Flagstaff, one crew over from where I was walking survey lines in the desert just outside of Las Vegas.

The chills that went up my spine followed me all the way home to where I was camping in the—unlockable—camper shell of my Toyota Tacoma, the dusty wind howling around its thin metal shell all night.

Listen, I wanted to make money for road tripping as much as the next girl, but exactly where did that finger come from? And where was the rest of that woman’s body? And why—where—but—didn’t they have police down here?

The questions were more plentiful than the answers. As the years in the Mojave cropped up and the body count rose along them, we never did hear the stories behind any of the human remains we turned in. Not the multiple skulls, not the drifter we found outside of Nipton with his uncashed welfare check in his pocket, not the “suicide” that I still swear was a very thinly-veiled mob hit (details redacted for the safety of the bios who found it). There were so many bodies found by tortoise biologists that eventually Outside Magazine did a feature on the phenomenon, though they didn’t cover half the tales I could have told.

One that stuck with me was three graves, complete with crosses and mounded dirt, armored with river-smoothed stones. We found them near an abandoned compound that used to house a meth lab, and a cult. Since five girls had gone missing in this area the local police in this case actually sent a crew out to exhume the sites. They dug them all the way to bedrock and found nothing, which always tickled my imagination.

I understand setting up crosses for a memorial, perhaps, but why go to the trouble to mound the dirt? Why lug so many stones in such a sweaty climate if you weren’t faking the graves for someone else’s benefit? I couldn’t stop thinking about it, and I never got answers, so I ended up writing a flash fiction story to give myself the resolution that reality was reluctant to allow me.

The sluggishness of the authorities when it came to following our GPS coordinates to the corpses gave me a healthy respect for how much easier it was to get away with murder than I had previously thought, at least in the Mojave. The desert always felt like a place real adults had forgotten. What with its abandoned and half-burnt trailers jutting up alongside the sand-drifted highways and the graffiti laced bones of defunct water parks.

That’s why when I decided to write a book about a female serial killer, I set her story in the Phoenix desert. Because I wanted the metaphorical resonance of her rising from the ashes of her past, sure. But mostly because I wanted somewhere to hide the bodies.

I started writing this book in a desert, of course. When I was working a job outside of Barstow fence monitoring. Just me walking miles of fence to look for distressed tortoises not used to having their habitat chopped up by the dividing lines of men. On a day when I’d just written one of the first chapters from my serial killer’s POV, I found two murder weapons.

Do I know they were murder weapons? Of course not. When I called the police, they said it was county jurisdiction and hung up on me. The two young county sheriffs who eventually responded had to borrow a set of my latex gloves for tortoise handling just to take the guns into evidence, and never followed up with me about the results of the investigation, if they even did one.

But guns like these cost hundreds to thousands of dollars. Why toss them out the window unless you had to?

I never learned who the guns belonged to, or how they got there. What I did learn was that if you want to get away with murder, you better do it in the desert.

Nika Grace loves writing fight scenes and kissing scenes and is always on the lookout for a story idea wild enough to include both. By day, she works as a writing coach with Sanctuary Editorial, and on the weekends, she and her husband love to disappear into the labyrinth of the canyon country in the American Southwest. Her home base is in Moab, Utah, but her muse lives in New Orleans. She is the author of Serial Killer Wanted.

Today, a federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Halima Salman, 27, a U.S. citizen and former resident of Brooklyn, also known as “Umm Khattab al-Muhajir,” of receiving military-type training from the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS), a designated foreign terrorist organization, in Syria. Salman was convicted after a two-week trial before U.S. District Judge Natasha C. Merle.

“The atrocities committed by ISIS, including mass executions, sexual slavery, and the systematic terrorizing of civilian populations, represent some of the gravest crimes of our time,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “There is simply no excuse for aligning with or receiving military training from an organization responsible for such suffering. Today's verdict sends a clear message that those who support this death cult will be found and prosecuted.”

“With today’s verdict, Salman is held accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “ISIS ravaged Syria and caused havoc across the globe; our Office will continue to prosecute those who supported its murderous reign.”

“It’s been nearly a decade since Halima Salman sought military training from ISIS in Syria, and today justice has been served,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI remains unwavering in its vigilance. We will continue to identify, disrupt, and bring to justice those who support foreign terrorist organizations and threaten the safety of our nation and our communities.”

As proven at trial, in September and October 2016, Salman’s parents traveled with her and her eight siblings out of the United States, ultimately destined for ISIS-controlled territory in Syria.

In late 2016 or early 2017, Salman was 18 years old and married to an ISIS fighter in Syria, where she voluntarily sought military-type training and received authorization to carry ammunition and an assault rifle from ISIS. Salman received a document certifying that she successfully completed that training, a copy of which was found on her husband’s cellphone after it was recovered from the battlefield. Also on her husband’s device were photos depicting Salman with an ISIS flag in the background and a video that shows her brandishing an AK-47 rifle.

The case was investigated by the FBI New York Field Office. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided significant assistance obtaining evidence overseas.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Adam Amir and Amanda Shami for the Eastern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Reich, Paralegal Specialist Emily Woodruff and Trial Attorney Patrick Cashman of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

#7712. Remembering Mark Pryor, beloved crime novelist and iconic Austinite

On October 8th, we lost Mark Pryor, a great craftsman of entertaining mysteries and thrillers, and an active and much loved member of the crime fiction community. He conceived unique heroes and anti-heroes with vivid settings. Not only was he a writer we admired, he was one we called a good friend.

His story was cool before he was even born. His father travelled on motorcycle across America on holiday from Britain where fell in love and brought the American lady home to marry. Mark and born and grew up in England with a love of soccer, where he studied journalism, then law. He used his dual citizenship to make a home in Austin, Texas where he practiced law as a prosecutor, mainly in Juvenile Court, and later as a defense attorney. He most valued his time with juvenile law, feeling he had leeway to hopefully get the perpetrator’s life back on track as well as get justice. However, what he valued most was his wife Sarah and three children, Blake, Henry, and Nicola.

His first novel, The Bookseller, he introduced us to Hugo Marston, the character he wrote about the most. Hugo, a former FBI profiler from Texas, worked as the chief of security for our embassy in Paris. When not indulging in his love of collecting and reading books, he finds himself dealing in mysteries often involving international intrigue. He is often assisted by his wild card of a CIA-connected buddy, Tom Green, his sometime girlfriend, French journalist Claudia Roux, and Parisian cop Lt. Camille Laurens, one of the first reoccurring trans characters in a mystery series to be written with dignity.

“He didn’t give readers a superficial tourist’s version of France,” explains James Ziskin, a friend who started out with him, roughly the same time when they were label mates at Seventh Street. “He wrote details that only an habitué would think to include. He knew the locations, the history, the language, and day-to-day minutiae that make a foreign setting ring true. Second, he was fearless in drawing his characters, for example Camille Laurens, a transgender police lieutenant who appears in several of the Hugo Marston books. It would have been much safer to write a policewoman or policeman. Then there’s his knowledge of the law, his sense of justice, and the expert plotting that runs through all his books. He was a gifted wordsmith, too.”

“His imagery was always so vivid,” adds friend and fellow writer, Puja Guha. “He could set the scene of where things were in a case, or how something happened along the Seine, or anywhere else, in a way that just made you see it in your head so clearly.”

Mark presented Hugo with just a few touches on his background, then revealing a little more with each book. However, he proved to be fully formed as Puja explains. “Hugo’s a great hero. Strong, capable, but also vulnerable and emotional. A really well-rounded character. I always just wished he could find real love in the series!”

His next protagonist, Dominic,  proved to a complete opposite. Like Mark he worked as a juvenile prosecutor in Austin, but he was also a musician, as well as a dangerous sociopath. The books are a bitter, but oh so sweet, a dark chocolate mix of Richard Stark, Jim Thompson, and Patricia Highsmith. (For the record, Mark had only read Highsmith before he wrote the first book, Hollow Man.) When the two of us had dinner one night with noir queens Megan Abbott and Alison Gaylin, he listened intently while we talked about the genre. He later told me he was taking notes that evening for the book. When I asked if he ever thought of doing a book where he pitted Hugo and Dominic in a book, he told me if he was being true to the characters, Hugo could probably survive two chapters.

His last series lead, Henri Lefort, turned out to be his most complex. Introduced in Die Around Sundown, Henri, a homicide detective with a past, works the streets of recently occupied Paris. With small historical details and rich characterizations, he depicts the emotions and humiliation of living in a conquered society. He does have fun putting him in the same apartment Hugo will reside in in the future.

Recently, he returned to Hugo with The Most Mysterious Bookshop in Paris. Hugo retires from the embassy to open up his own bookshop. It opens with a beautiful passage with Hugo taking a morning stroll to the store, taking in the poetic glory of the city that reflects mark’s love for it. Of course, his old skills and reputation pull him in when he is asked to help a chocolate maker faced with blackmail. He delves into the making of the confections with fascinating detail. Many of the supporting cast returns. Pryor finished a second book, A Vintage Murder In Paris, that will be published in spring.

Mark was one of the most sociable writers I ever worked with. He often asked to tag along for dinners I’d have with authors who came into town for book events. One of these dinners led to a strong friendship he had with Phillip Kerr. He was a mainstay at Bouchercon, beloved by both authors and fans, all drawn to his charm and dry wit. To be around the god natured ribbing between James and Mark of who was the better author was hilarious. “I loved sparring with Mark. Of course, Mark landed more blows than he received, I can tell you that. He could slice you to pieces with his wit, and make you laugh at yourself anyway. We used to insult each other publicly whenever we got the chance, but it was all in good fun.“

Fellow Austin author, Mike McCrary described his personality in a nutshell. “Mark was the person you wanted to sit next to at that boring dinner. The one you hoped would be at the thing you didn’t want go to because he’d make it fun. He always made me laugh and rarely caught him without a smile.”

“He had the most mischievous smile,” says Ziskin.  “That English accent. His generosity. His willingness to protect victims and champion the underdog. And, of course, his sense of humor. Everyone liked Mark.”

Mike recalls his mischievous one evening. “Noir at the Bar in Austin. A great example of his wit and his never-ending push to play with the unexpected. He went up on stage before me and he knew I was next. As he wrapped up he turned to the audience and said, “Be nice to Mike. He’s not used to crowds this big.”

One of my favorite memories of Mark is when I hung out with him at a Bouchercon opening party. He had a little too much to drink that evening and was feeling pretty loose. When he saw me the next morning he said with all sincerity and Cary Grant charm, “You were with me most of the night, who do I need to apologize to?”

“I feel like we became close friends after our first couple of conversations,” recalls Puja. “He always made sure no one felt left out and brought people into the discussion.”

He encouraged his fellow authors, reminding us that we were all in this together and we should take pride in what we can do in crime fiction and if you were friend, you knew you had someone who always had your back. He often helped out people who had legal questions about there book. He used Mr. Ziskin’s skills to do both a map and fictional family tree in two of his Hugo books. “Mark mentioned that he liked a map that had appeared in one of my books, so I told him I’d drawn it and offered to do one for him if he wanted. He told me which landmarks he wanted to include and I did my best. The family tree must have come about in the same way. It was something you do gladly for a friend.”

He used his books as a way to show his love for others. He often roped his kids into making funny promo videos. Many of his friends’ names popped up in his books for characters. I believe one of the reasons he turned Hugo into a bookseller was so he could namecheck his colleagues and promote their books in his own. With Mark, everyone was welcome in his world, whether the real or fictional one.

A legendary crime bookseller, Scott Montgomery runs The Hard Word blog, https://www.thehardword.me. Always a crime fiction fan, Scott Montgomery worked on the sales staff of the acclaimed and influential The Mystery Bookstore in Los Angeles for four years.

#7711. DEI attacks are likely to refine and improve programs, experts say

The intense pressure to end diversity initiatives has led companies to scrutinize their policies. Many of the attacks will end up strengthening DEI programs.

The politicians, provocateurs and think tanks that in the past few years have worked to dismantle diversity, equity and inclusion may not appreciate the full consequences of their efforts.

They’ve used a variety of tactics, in the public and private sectors, including White House executive orders; lawsuits or the threat of lawsuits; shareholder proposals; and needling on social media. They’ve notched high-profile wins, most notably the Supreme Court’s ruling against affirmative action and capitulation at several companies, including retailers and brands that have ended or scaled back their DEI programs.

The successful challenges, inevitably, are forcing scrutiny of DEI practices. But they also provide an opportunity to reinforce DEI goals and execution, which David Glasgow, executive director of New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging, sees as a silver lining.

Indeed, the victories are hardly universal. Because diversity, equity and inclusion are good for business for a variety of reasons, most companies are not abandoning DEI. So far in 2025, Target, Nike and Costco are among those that have defended at least some aspects of their policies (in Costco’s case, vociferously). As the Heritage Foundation, a major DEI foe, noted in November, most Fortune 500 companies continue to publicly commit to DEI.

“It is a time for companies to refine and strengthen their inclusion efforts in ways that reduce the risk in the short term — because the risk is real, and we know that — and in ways that are sustainable in the long term,” said Adrienne Pulido, vice president of inclusion insights at Kantar. “So it is looking at both ends of the spectrum, in terms of being very clear about what inclusion means to their business.”

DEI is being pilloried as discriminatory and unfair, yet these systems are designed to create a business that is neither. That is, a business where employees have a variety of backgrounds and perspectives (diversity); hiring, promotion and other actions are executed fairly (equity); and the culture is comfortable and inviting to all who work there (inclusion).

“Unpacking what DEI is and what inclusion is, is part of this moment we're in and part of the conversation that companies need to have about their strategies,” Pulido said by video conference. “What does DEI mean to the business itself? What does it mean to the business and to the future business? Because the demographics of the country are changing, and our research shows that inclusion as a concept, as an idea, is very popular among Americans of all backgrounds.”

DEI goals for most companies are more important than ever because the markets for their products and services are more diverse than they were a decade or more ago, according to Effenus Henderson, who has worked in recruiting, staffing and succession planning at companies in the U.S. and abroad since the 1970s.

“This attack is amplified through the use of social media and technology and psychometrics, where emotions get aroused and reinforced,” he said by phone. “But fundamental to all this is that DEI is not about creating systems that are discriminatory, or about quotas, or a focus on one thing at the exclusion of others. I don't think organizations have really done that. What they have been doing is really trying to expand participation because of the growing demographic change that we're seeing.”

The need to develop DEI strategies that fit with and further business strategies dictates the involvement of leadership, according to Henderson. Too often, though, they are left to the human resources department, leaving companies at risk of adopting DEI programming that is ineffective and possibly indefensible.

“The companies that are able to navigate this generally are the ones where leadership has spent the time talking about it,” he said. “It's not just about reacting to the George Floyd situation or to civil rights laws or litigation. It's really, ‘How do we integrate this as a part of the DNA of who we are as an organization?’ If your organization is more performative, then they don't really understand how it helps to shape business strategy and policy.”

DEI should be treated like any other strategic priority, according to Tim Heneveld, country director for Pergolux in North America. With DEI under the spotlight, it’s a good moment to reassess whether hiring, workplace environment, leadership and operational strategies fit with broader aims.

“That means setting measurable goals, using data to track impact, and holding leadership accountable,” Heneveld said by email. “Some organizations are feeling pressure to scale back DEI, but I think doing so would be shortsighted. Instead, companies should refine their DEI strategies, aligning them with long-term business goals rather than reacting to what they are seeing in the media or any other outside factors. I've experienced, firsthand, workplaces can attract top talent, strengthen their teams, and improve retention.”

In some cases, companies are continuing with their DEI efforts, but changing the names of their initiatives or titles of their employees, experts said.

Crafting DEI initiatives and training is always a work in progress because businesses, markets and demographics evolve, according to Henderson. For many companies, that may mean avoiding those three letters of the alphabet, or the words “diversity, equity and inclusion.” But that, too, requires some thought, he said.

“Is continuing to refer to it under those banners still appropriate, and if I look at renaming it, am I doing that to help enhance our appeal to the markets of the customers and employees we serve? Are we doing it as a reactive, defensive thing for a short-term issue that's hot and heavy right now?” he said. “Get clarity around your objectives, the alignment with your strategies, and then decide whether how you are framing it today will work for you tomorrow and the day after. At some companies, it may mean one thing, and to others it may mean something else.”

The list of lawsuits against DEI programs tracked by the Meltzer Center is long, and getting longer.

Most of these claims invoke civil rights laws intended to end or prevent unfair hiring practices or contracts. Frequently that includes Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, barring discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin; Section 1981 of the federal code barring discrimination in contracts; and the U.S. Constitution’s equal protection clause, according to Glasgow. The Meltzer Center advises companies to avoid DEI practices that give preference to members of certain groups and involve a tangible benefit.

Evaluating whether a company’s DEI programs run afoul of the latest interpretations of these codes entails enlisting attorneys or other compliance experts.

“This has become a thriving legal practice area,” Glasgow said.

Any business strategy should always be grounded in risk mitigation, and this is just another place for companies to check, according to Henderson. Companies may learn that, to avoid risk, certain aspects of their DEI programs should change.

Others may find that they pass muster. In its proxy statement urging shareholders to vote against a proposal that could have weakened its DEI programs, Costco’s board of directors made clear that the retailer regularly evaluates its “practices concerning compliance with law, including evolving Supreme Court decisions.”

In describing how Costco obeys the law and does not discriminate in hiring, promotion and other practices, the board also provided a litany of protected statuses. This is a reminder that, while civil rights statutes are being leveraged to overturn DEI practices, they nevertheless do bar discrimination for a host of reasons. Moreover, any company that does business abroad will encounter antidiscrimination law that isn’t being disrupted by political activism the way it is in the U.S., Henderson said.

“If you look at Canada, Europe, Asia and South America, there are regulations and laws that support and value diversity,” he said. “So backing away from DEI may, in fact, create harm for your business strategies in other parts of the world. It's not a simple answer, and it just depends on who you are.”

While it may seem like DEI programs are quickly getting scrapped in order to avoid controversy, most are simply under review, Glasgow and others said.

“I think it's prompting a much deeper reflection within companies, not just on what is strictly legal or illegal in what we're doing, but on what has been working and what has not been working,” Glasgow said. “Could we be doing this work more effectively, in a way that actually helps us achieve our business goals, or helps us create the kind of culture that we want to create? Are there things that have been low impact, or maybe even have a negative impact, that we should get rid of, even if it's not for legal reasons? I think the moment that we're living in now could be a helpful reset moment for the field.”

#7710. Judge who repeatedly used racist slur removed by court

A judge in upstate New York was removed from the bench Tuesday by the New York Court of Appeals, the state’s highest court, for repeatedly using a racial slur while recounting a personal story and making other racially insensitive comments. (Image from Shutterstock)

A judge in upstate New York was removed from the bench Tuesday by the New York Court of Appeals, the state’s highest court, for repeatedly using a racial slur while recounting a personal story and making other racially insensitive comments.

Judge Walter W. Jones of Canandaigua, New York, used the N-word at least three times during a conversation with a court staff member and a public defender outside the courtroom in May 2024. Jones, who is white, was telling a story about a Black man who had worked in his grandfather’s cotton fields in Texas, according to the court.

Jones said in a court hearing he used the slur just one time because he was quoting his father, whom he described as “racist.”

In affirming the New York State Commission on Judicial Conduct, the appeals court noted that Jones also made racially insensitive remarks during the arraignment of a Black defendant, saying she had “played the race card” when she accused him of setting her bail too high because she was Black.

The racial slur that Jones used “was unquestionably offensive and was followed just days later” by his “racially biased, on-the-record comments regarding a Black defendant who had appeared before him,” the appeals court wrote in its ruling.

Jones’ “inability to recognize the impact that his statements could have on the public’s confidence in the judiciary’s impartiality and integrity demonstrates his lack of understanding of the need for judges ‘to both be and appear to be impartial,’” the appeals court said.

Jones was first elected as a town justice in Canandaigua, located in the Finger Lakes region of western New York, in 1999, according to a story by the New York Times.

#7709. A Writer’s Night at America’s Most Haunted Hotel

Book tours have taught me to expect the unexpected. There was the couple in Texas who kindly housed me but warned about their vicious late-night, door-opening, biting cat, and the time a prominent politician’s son asked me to edit his “fictional novel,” a thinly-veiled story about his father’s real-life exploits. But nothing prepared me for what happened in Eureka Springs, Arkansas.

I’d recently met the fabulous writer Stephanie Storey while she was touring her beautiful debut novel Oil and Marble. Stephanie grew up in Arkansas, and I’m pretty sure she told the director of the literary festival, Books in Bloom, about me. I received an invitation to be a featured author at the festival in the spring of 2018. I’d never been to Arkansas and was excited to experience both the town and this celebration of literature. My communication from the director stated I’d be staying at the Crescent, a historic hotel founded in 1866. The town was as adorable and welcoming as advertised, a Victorian village with rumored healing springs, and everyone I met exuded warmth and hospitality. The thriving literary community radiated kindness and engagement.

My room was comfy and oddly shaped, the kind of space that had clearly remained much as it was in the 1800s. The quirks of the layout only added to its charm. It wasn’t until I checked in that day that I noticed a sign proclaiming the hotel to be “America’s Most Haunted Hotel.” I’m not easily spooked, but I do have a healthy curiosity and respect for possibilities.

That evening, after going out for dinner with several other authors from the festival, I took the stairs rather than the elevator to get some exercise as I made my way back to my room. When I reached my floor, I noticed a throng of people blocking the hallway. As I got closer, I realized they were listening with rapt attention to a hotel employee leading them on the nightly ghost tour. And then it hit me: they were standing directly outside my room. The tour guide was calling my room the most haunted room in the hotel.

I looked around, half-expecting someone to jump out and shout, Gotcha! You shoulda seen your face! But no. I eased closer to listen, catching fragments of the guide’s narrative: something about a secret pregnancy, a woman who had mysteriously fallen—or perhaps jumped—from the window of the very room where I’d be sleeping that night. The group murmured, a young girl chewed her nail, a man snapped a photo of my door, and then they moved on down the hall, leaving me standing there. I said aloud to no one, Are you kidding me?

That night, I settled into bed, read for a while, and then turned off the lamp. I wasn’t particularly concerned about the ghost tour’s commentary. After all, the guide was doing his job, creating atmosphere and mystery to justify the tour fee. My room was cozy and funky, and I liked the bed. I nestled into the sheets, closed my eyes, and drifted off.

Then, almost immediately, I sensed a cat hopping onto the bed. Now, I know that sounds wacky. And I can’t exactly articulate the sensation. Still, if you’ve ever had a cat, you know that particular feeling—the gentle padding of paws, the slight shifting of the comforter, barely perceptible but unmistakable. This felt so real, so present, that I jumped up and turned on the lamp, sending my reading glasses flying off the nightstand. There was no cat on my bed. I looked underneath, checked the bathroom, searched the corners of the room, all the while calling Here, kitty kitty, my suspension of disbelief tested. Absolutely nothing.

I got back into bed, turned off the light, and lay there, mind racing, acutely aware of every shadow and sound. I thought of my youngest child, a seventh grader, back home in South Carolina. He had a big math test the next day. I turned the lamp back on and grabbed my phone to text him a good luck, good night text. Not eager to get back out of bed to retrieve my glasses, I squinted and pecked out my message.

“Night, buddy. Proud of you. You got this! Love you so much.”

I hit send, turned off the lamp, then, oddly enough, slept soundly. The next morning, I awoke early and absentmindedly picked up my glasses, only to realize, with great embarrassment, that my late-night text had not been to my son Will, but to my longtime OB-GYN, Dr. Robert. Mortified, I typed a quick explanation. I kept it simple: “Oops. Wrong recipient. Meant for my son.” He replied with a crying-laughing emoji. Thank goodness my gynecologist had a sense of humor.

I opened my laptop and prepped for my session at the festival later that morning. Sipping my coffee, curiosity got the better of me. On a whim, I googled “ghost cat of Crescent Hotel, Eureka Springs,” not really expecting to find anything.

There was, in fact, a ghost cat at the Crescent Hotel—and it had a name: Morris. He was a real orange tabby who had lived at the hotel for twenty-one years, supposedly serving as its unofficial general manager. He had an office with his title on the door and a custom cat-door cut into the lobby so he could move freely through the hotel. When Morris died in 1994, over three hundred people attended his funeral. He was buried on the hotel’s East Lawn with a headstone.

According to what I found, Morris apparently loved his job too much to leave. Guests and staff continued to report his presence—a cat brushing past ankles, faint meows in empty hallways, and, you guessed it: a gentle weight on the bed.

I hadn’t experienced the ghost of a tragic woman in the most haunted room, but I may have experienced Morris.

As I left the hotel that morning to start my day at the festival, I stepped outside and visited Morris’s grave. Standing there, I thought about what it means to be a writer—to remain open to possibilities, to imagine. Morris’s late-night visit had broadened my lens. And as unexpected situations tend to do, the experience made me consider a new what-if. A cat so devoted to his purpose that he transcended death itself to continue his work? There was a story in that.

There always is, if you’re willing to see it.

Fig Days (on-sale April 6, 2027; Regal House Publishing)

Born in Charleston and raised on Johns Island, Michel Stone is part of the 11th generation of her family to hail from the South Carolina Lowcountry. She is the author of the novels Fig Days, forthcoming from Regal House Publishing on April 6, 2027, Border Child (Doubleday), and The Iguana Tree (Hub City Press). She is the winner of the Mary Frances Hobson Prize for Distinguished Achievement in Arts and Letters, the Patricia Winn Award for Southern Literature, and the South Carolina Fiction Award. Michel’s novels have been widely, favorably reviewed from The San Francisco Chronicle to The New Yorker. She holds a BA in English from Clemson University and an M.Ed. from Converse College. Michel is a Fellow of the Aspen Global Leadership Network, a Liberty Fellow, and a Ucross Fellow. She spends as much time as possible in her beloved Lowcountry with her family and Boykin Spaniel. Visit Michel online at michelstone.com and on Instagram @michel.stone.writes.

#7707. Suspenseful not-exactly-horror movies to watch, this Halloween

I don’t know if I like horror or not, honestly. I definitely like it more than I used to? Still, I don’t really ever want to turn on a movie that’s going to scare me. I like thrills, maybe a few chills… that’s it. So, here are some good Halloween movies that are very suspenseful and even a bit spooky and maybe even a little scary… but that won’t traumatize you. I think?

I grouped them into three categories: old-timey suspense movies, movies that definitely have blood but aren’t GORY scary messes (the blood volume is offset by inventiveness or funniness or satire), and then movies that I could sit through but that are definitely too scary for some people.

NOT VERY SCARY, AS IN “SCARY IN AN OLD-FASHIONED WAY”:

I’m not talking about the insipid remake with Armie Hammer, but the original, Alfred Hitchcock’s masterpiece. The good people who read CrimeReads do not need me to tell them to watch Rebecca, but I’m underscoring it because watching a scene in which a house burns down might be the very thing you need, lately, idk.

I will never, never stop praising Charles Laughton’s only film, a masterpiece about a psychopathic serial-killer and self-appointed preacher (Robert Mitchum, always great, never better), who, when he gets out of jail, becomes obsessed with finding the money hidden by his lately-executed bank robber former-cellmate—a secret which is kept by the robber’s two young children. TELL ME this is not the most eye-widening plot you’ve ever heard. And now believe me when I say that it is shot gorgeously, too. The cinematography will make you scream. SWOOPING shadows. Ghostly UNDERWATER shots. Insane stuff.

My high school AP US History teacher Mr. O’Neill heartily recommended that I watch this earlyish-career Hitchcock movie, about a teenage girl (Teresa Wright) who becomes suspicious that her beloved Uncle Charley (Joseph Cotten) is a murderer, after he visits her family in their idyllic California town. It’s really excellent—Mr. O’Neill was correct.

Based on the novel by Boileau-Narcejac (a pair of writers, actually), this midcentury horror-noir from one of my favorite directors, Henri-Georges Clouzot, is the perfect Halloween movie. Simone Signoret and Véra Clouzot play the mistress and wife (respectively) of a sadistic schoolmaster (Paul Meurisse) who plan the perfect murder to rid their lives of him. But when the murder is done and his body vanishes, the tables begin to turn. It’s excellent, absolutely chilling feature—the best film Hitchcock never made (and, IMO, better than most films Hitchcock did make). (This is just an enthusiastic endorsement… I’m not knocking Hitchcock.)

Richard (Cornel Wilde) is a writer who believes he’s struck gold when he encounters Ellen Berent (Gene Tierney), a gorgeous young woman who is totally infatuated with him. Turns out, though, that she’s an obsessive psychopath. Whoops!

Park Chan-wook’s black comedy-thriller is one of the best movies about “hitting a breaking point” ever made. I love a satire about capitalism, and this movie, about a middle-class, white-collar worker who gets laid off and subsequently goes on a murder spree to get rid of anyone who might be competition for his old job, is pretty perfect.

I feel like no one saw Resurrection, an engrossing, chilling thriller starring Rebecca Hall and Tim Roth, and this is a crime. It might seem somewhat standard in plot—it is about a woman whose life is upended when a figure from her past returns—but it is punched up by fantastic performances: Roth’s sinister calmness and Hall’s detonating desperation. She also gives maybe the single best scene performance of the year: a seven-minute, one-take monologue that she delivers with her entire face. Incredible.

I’ll say upfront that M. Night Shyamalan’s Trap isn’t perfect. There are the kind of pitfalls that always seem to pop up in Shyamalan’s movies (a tendency to over-explain some things, some strange or stilted dialogue), but I find these things less “pitfalls” than funny markers of style. Shyamalan is an auteur in the truest sense of the word, and, in an era of endless sequels and unwanted franchises, I find it a breath of fresh air that he always seems able to turn out a new, original idea. And Trap, which is a movie about a serial killer who realizes that the FBI are closing in on him while he takes his tween daughter to a Taylor Swift-style pop concert, is not only a delightful and original premise, but it is also executed with such love and care that it feels almost impossible not to enjoy.

First and foremost, it is a father-daughter movie. Our protagonist, the slick murderer Cooper (Josh Hartnett), adores his young daughter Riley (Ariel Donoghue), and is so excited to be able to be with her to enjoy her favorite artist, the pop singer Lady Raven (Saleka Shyamalan). His clear love for her and his family plays out nicely against his increasing need for self-preservation; as the walls begin to close in, he clings tight to his daughter, and it’s clear that for maybe the first time, he’s beginning to worry if this will be a day his daughter won’t forget not for its specialness, but its potential to upend her life. And second, Shyamalan’s own daughter Saleka, herself a singer-songwriter and musician, plays such a large part in this film, that it is clear that Trap is a family-affair, behind the scenes just as much as in front of the camera. I find it incredibly charming that, at the start of Shyamalan’s career, he was marketed as an extremely mysterious figure with a dark imagination, and now, maybe years later, he is perhaps most famous for seeming to be a very loving father.

Oh, one more thing… in Trap, there is an FBI agent/criminal profiler who is leading the manhunt, and she’s played by the great Hayley Mills. Hayley Mills is the former child star who played the original twins in the original version of The Parent Trap (1961). So, like, I can’t stop thinking about how M. Night Shyamalan cast the original parent-trapper in the original Parent Trap to lay a parent trap to trap a parent in Trap.

Drian De Palma’s Blow Out is a clever re-imagining of Michelangelo Antonioni’s Blow Up (the film listed right above), only featuring an a movie sound engineer (John Travolta) accidentally recording a murder, rather than catching it on film. This film has a lot to say about what surveillance, scandal, and murder have to do with America—and thus it’s set in Philadelphia during the Fourth of July.

I loved this wonderful, twisty satirical film about our… cough… reliance on technology. I can’t say much more than that; but it’s an excellent film for today’s modern age.

Maybe you’re not interested in extremely well-made parodies of Gen-Z online culture, and maybe you are. But it would still be worth your time to watch Halina Reijn’s Bodies Bodies Bodies, about a group of narcissistic zoomers stuck in a mansion together during a hurricane, playing a murder-themed party game that somehow becomes real. The kids start to suspect each other, in ways that provide ample opportunities to satirize the “toxic” fake-woke culture permeating the zeitgeist and wielded by the most privileged among us.

I absolutely loved Strange Darling, JT Mollner’s wild and weird serial killer movie, which was shot all on 35 mm film by the actor-turned-cinematographer Giovanni Ribisi. And man, he’s a good DP. Strange Darling is as much as a visual treat as it is a narrative extravaganza, a fully controlled and impressive story told in an innovative way. It stars a superb Willa Fitzgerald as a young woman (simply called “the lady”) and an impressive Kyle Gallner (simply called “the demon”) and it drops us in the middle of their night, a night that has started as a one night stand and has twisted into a terrifying cat-and-mouse chase puppeted by a serial killer. The shot that plays during the opening credits, of Fitzgerald’s character running desperately across a green field in bright red scrubs, her ear having been blasted off by a shotgun, is one of the most arresting things I’ve seen at the movies in a while. And the movie only gets more, well, arresting from there.

Would a list about small-town crime movies be complete without an entry from David Lynch? No! Kyle MacLachlan is a young college student returning to his hometown for the season when he discovers a severed human ear in a cornfield (I KNOW!), and thus embarks on a strange mystery.

I loved this frosty, bloody, bone-chilling indie film, written and directed by Bridget Savage Cole and Danielle Krudy. It’s about two sisters (Sophie Lowe and Morgan Saylor) from a small, coastal New England fishing town. Shortly after the death of their beloved mother, they wind up having to cover up the terrible murder of a would-be assaulter. But as they attempt to conceal the crime, hoping friendly police officers and nosy neighbors do not suspect anything too fishy, they become drawn into their town’s dark underbelly, which turns out to be surprisingly matriarchal.

I loved this comic slasher film, starring Samara Weaving as a young woman marrying into a billionaire family dynasty without realizing they’re going to wind up attempting to sacrifice her at midnight on her wedding night. It’s a wonderful satire on elitism and class in America, and a fun (sometimes heavy-handed) take-down of patriarchal institutions in general. If you’re looking something to watch with a friend, I highly suggest this. I saw this with my friend Eleni in theaters, last summer, and we sat in the last row and ate doughnuts the whole time. The movie will make your blood run cold at times, but this memory warms my heart.

A sequel that is just as good as/if not better than its original, Ready or Not II pops into the days after the events of Ready or Not I. It’s very Halloween 2. In this sequel, after she’s made it through, she’s challenged by a powerful group connected to her in-laws’ family (also with a Satanic pact) to a DOUBLE OR NOTHING game of hide-and-seek, and they have to play, or they’ll kill her sister, Kathryn Newton! The actors in this group of deadly players include such luminaries as Sarah Michelle Gellar, Elijah Wood, Néstor Carbonell, Kevin Durand… and David Cronenberg. Yes, David Cronenberg. DO! A! DOUBLE! FEATURE!

I debated with a friend whether or not this Barton Fink is a proper crime movie (I think it qualifies for this list because it’s ALL about L.A. in the summer and it’s probably the sweatiest film ever made, plus there is also a vicious murder in the middle of it) but he thinks not a crime movie as much as a terrifying, vaguely supernatural movie about a mental breakdown. Still… decide for yourself.

No, this is not The Watcher, the incompetent Netflix series adapting that one article in The Cut. This is Chloe Okuno’s gutting, sensitive, all-too-real movie about a young woman who discovers that she has a stalker. When Julia (an amazing Maika Monroe) movies with her husband to Bucharest, she thinks that the man who often stares out at her from the apartment across the street could be the serial killer who has been decapitating women around the city.

Eileen! This thriller, which is basically perfect almost all of the way through, is based on the novel by Ottessa Moshfegh. Anne Hathaway rocks her portrayal of a sultry, secretive psychologist at a young men’s prison in Massachusetts. She, Rebecca, is the first bright spot in a while that Eileen (Thomasin McKenzie), who works in the prison, has experienced, and it’s not long before Eileen begins to grow veeeeeery interested in her. The movie builds well and is really interesting, but a late-in-the-film monologue from Marin Ireland brings the house down.

OKAY THIS ARE ACTUALLY DEFINITELY A BIT SCARY BUT YOU WILL PROBABLY BE OKAY (PROBABLY):

Late Night with the Devil is a fresh, bracing horror film from writer-directors Cameron and Colin Cairnes and producer-star David Dastmalchian. It has a crystalline premise. Get a load of this: a late night TV show host, desperate for better ratings, plans a broadcast that will catch audiences’ attentions. His program, which airs on Halloween night in 1977, includes appearances from psychics, paranormal debunkers, and a psychologist who claims to have been able to communicate with a demon inhabiting a possessed child. Oh, and… the possessed child, herself. She’s there too. So, of course, when the show commences, things go horribly wrong. The film unfolds crisply, playing with a cinéma vérité style, as if we’re watching a behind-the-scenes broadcast about the apparently-famed broadcast, which includes material never before seen. I love films that handle exposition creatively, and this one certainly does, though its sense of overarching structure does fade a bit as the film progresses (sometimes, later on, I wasn’t positive if we were watching the broadcast, the broadcast of the broadcast, or something else). Perhaps this is related, but at times (in the film’s revelatory third act, for example) it’s almost too economical; I would not have called the film heavyhanded if it provided a few more conclusive answers. Just a couple! I mean, the devil’s in the details! But these are quibbles. Overall, it’s a smartly-paced, original, and riveting horror movie. If you like scary movies of any kind, or if you like the very specific category of “movies about broadcast television,” this one’s for you.

I am a moderate horror movie fan married to an extreme horror movie fan, so my consumption of all things spooky is pretty constant throughout the year. Still, I can’t deny that it’s just more fun to watch something bone-chilling in the chilly days of October. This month, I recommend you find yourself a cozy blanket and a moderately brave loved one and watch The Invitation, a horror-thriller movie that takes place at a dinner party in the Hollywood Hills (I know—and it gets even scarier)! A man and his new girlfriend attend a dinner hosted by the man’s ex-husband and her new husband, along with a few other friends. Things get even more intense than you’d expect, and the final of the movie is one of the most haunting horror ending I’ve ever seen.—Jessie Gaynor

Suspiria (2018) As someone who prefers to peek into the cinematic world of horror every now and then (and especially in October), I couldn’t help but recommend Luca Guadagnino’s 2018 remake of the classic Suspiria, which cranks up palimpsestic, arthouse film aesthetics so high that you can occasionally forget you’re watching a scary movie. The film clocks in at almost three hours and features heavy-hitters like Tilda Swinton, Dakota Johnson, Alek Wek, Chole Grace Mortez, and Mia Goth. The muted wintery aesthetic is rightfully accompanied with slithering worms, broken bones, ghoulish breathing, the occasional jump-scare, and plenty of blood and guts to make your toes curl. And I mustn’t forget: the ending is so unexpected that you’ll feel you’ve just emerged from a fever dream (and that’s probably because—spoiler—it is and is not). Suspiria has all you need for, what will likely be, an intense night you won’t forget—or one you’ll hope not to remember. –Rasheeda Saka   The Invisible Man (2020) The Invisible Man updates the classic story of Griffin, a man who has turned himself invisible and winds up using this quality to deftly harm people. Yet unlike the 1933 film version (in turn based on H.H. Wells’s novel of the same name), Griffin is not a rampaging, murderous lunatic who endangers society, but a possessive and vengeful threat to one woman in particular. This theme rings a little familiar: don’t we hear often that women are more likely to be murdered by someone they know than by a random maniac? The new Invisible Man makes Griffin the abusive ex-boyfriend of our protagonist Cecilia (Elizabeth Moss). He seems to have died, but has really turned transparent, which makes his vicious stalking even easier to accomplish. Because of this, for a while, the new Invisible Man, written and directed by Leigh Whannell, seems like a straight-up, supernatural horror movie—in which a woman is haunted by a ghost rather than hunted by a person. The way the film allegorically uses genre in this way to starkly un-desensitize us (apologies for that turn of phrase) to abuse is generally pretty successful, but the film possibly makes its more intense criticism of patriarchal oppression through Cecilia’s attempt to prove that someone is literally stalking her. This is the least science-fictional and most gut-wrenchingly real part of the movie: that in attempting to prove that she is in danger, Cecilia would be fighting an uphill battle even if her assaulter were visible. And he’s not. (Available to stream on HBO Max.)

Olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. #7706. ABA tracks new challenges affecting Public Service Loan Forgiveness borrowers

The ABA is closely monitoring new problems affecting borrowers working toward loan forgiveness. (Image from Shutterstock)

For lawyers and other student loan borrowers working in public service jobs, the path to having their remaining federal student loan balances discharged under Public Service Loan Forgiveness program after 120 months of qualifying payments is becoming increasingly difficult to navigate.

Under the PSLF program, created by Congress in 2007 with the support of the ABA, borrowers who have made 120 timely payments on their federal direct loans while employed full time in qualifying public service jobs are eligible to receive forgiveness of whatever portion of their loan remains after completing the payments.

But the ABA is closely monitoring new problems affecting borrowers working toward loan forgiveness. Issues include processing delays, payment record errors, growing application backlogs, and changes in Department of Education policies and procedures—some implemented with little or no public notice. Significant staffing cuts at the department, including a 40% reduction in Federal Student Aid office staff, have added to concerns about whether problems can be resolved promptly.

For reasons that are not yet clear, many borrowers have not received credit for qualifying loan repayments they’ve made since June, which means those payments cannot yet be counted toward their 120-repayment requirement. The Department of Education has not offered information or explanation on the missing information.

Separately, the Department of Education confirmed in August that it has reduced the number of some borrowers’ qualifying payments, potentially delaying when their remaining loan balances will be forgiven. After initially describing the falling payment counts as a “data issue,” the department subsequently said the changes were intentional, correcting coding errors during the Biden administration that resulted in inaccurate payment counts for some borrowers.

For example, some of the PSLF credit reversals may have been for payments made in a repayment plan that didn’t qualify for PSLF, although without an explanation from the Education Department about this process, some borrowers believe their payment counts were removed erroneously.

Without a formal announcement, the department also in July quietly eliminated the Biden-era 15-day grace period on whether PSLF-eligible payments counted as timely. As of July 1, a payment must be made “on or before the due date” to count as a qualifying payment under PSLF.

Also, a “clarification” by the department about the PSLF Buyback program is causing confusion and concern among borrowers.

The PSLF Buyback program allows public service employees to get credit toward the required 120 payments for months their loans were, e.g., in deferment or forbearance and thus not eligible for PSLF. Borrowers can apply to “buy back” those months, however, by paying what they would have paid had they been in repayment during those months.

But under updated Department of Education guidance, borrowers will not be able to buy back credit for payments made while under either of two new repayment plans—the Repayment Assistance Plan or the Tiered Standard Repayment Plan. These two new repayment plans were created in legislation signed into law by President Donald Trump in 2025.

Further causing concern is the significant application backlog for the PSLF Buyback program. As of April, the application backlog was between 70,000 to 90,000, but no new data has been released since that time. Even if the backlog has been reduced, some borrowers have waited two years or more to get credit for retroactive payments. The delay requires them to remain in their jobs and repay their loans for longer than required, thus functionally ending the buyback program.

On Oct. 21, the Department of Justice dropped its appeal of two court rulings that stayed the Department of Education’s controversial proposed rules to PSLF, which would have narrowed PSLF eligibility by excluding employees of organizations engaged in activities the department considered as having a “substantially illegal purpose.”

In August, the department had appealed the separate decisions by federal judges in Massachusetts and Washington, D.C., that had vacated the rules.

The ABA vigorously opposed the department’s proposals. In letters to Secretary of Education Linda McMahon, ABA Presidents Bill Bay and Michelle Behnke cited a lack of statutory and other legal authority. The ABA House of Delegates reinforced that opposition through adoption of Resolution 505 at its February 2026 midyear meeting, which opposes efforts to politicize this politically neutral program.

“Any perception that benefits are awarded based on political affiliation or ideology undermines the legitimacy of programs such as PSLF, discourages participation, and decreases the requisite public confidence they require to be successful,” the report accompanying the resolution states.

The ABA recognizes the crucial role PSLF plays in encouraging individuals to pursue careers that provide much-needed public services, including public defense services and civil legal aid representation to underrepresented communities such as senior citizens and veterans.

Since the program’s creation, the ABA has consistently responded to attacks and efforts to repeal or cut the program, including direct lobbying efforts through multiple Congresses and administrations; major grassroots campaigns including as a priority at past ABA Day fly-in events in Washington, D.C.; and working alongside its allies in the PSLF Coalition, a collaboration of more than 100 nonprofit and public service organizations.

In all, the ABA has adopted three policies supporting the program, including one in 2002 calling for the program’s creation. The most recent, Resolution 505, urges removal of the requirement that applicants be in qualifying employment at the time of applying for discharge of their student loans—a current program requirement that holds borrowers in limbo, unable to change jobs until the paperwork is filed. Once the required service and payment obligations are met, the resolution states, “there should be no further obligation than to apply for the benefits owed.”

As new issues with the program continue to emerge, the ABA will continue to work with allies to identify issues affecting borrowers and press for solutions. To learn more as significant developments occur, follow us at @ABAGrassroots on LinkedIn.

This report is written by the ABA Governmental Affairs Office and discusses advocacy efforts by the ABA relating to issues being addressed by Congress and the executive branch of the U.S. government. Follow @ABAGrassroots on social media.

This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.
